title: 1. Grid drag preview repeats whole-state validation for an unchanged snapped position
details:
**Call path and trigger.** In edit mode, pointer movement reaches `updateDragPreview` from the DnD move/over handlers and collision-frame path in `grid-editor.tsx`. The handler snaps to a target grid coordinate and calls `previewGridMove`; only after the engine returns an accepted preview does it compare `active.lastPreviewKey` and skip publishing an unchanged preview. The resize path does this in the opposite order: `previewResize` checks the key before `previewGridResize`.

`previewGridMove` clones the transactional grid state and validates it. `validateGridState` scans placements and checks every placement against the remainder of its grid, making overlap validation quadratic in the placements within each grid. The call repeats on pointer/DnD events even when the snapped target coordinate has not changed. This is avoidable CPU work and transient per-event object allocation, not retained RAM or a leak.

**Smallest compatible fix.** After computing the candidate preview key, check whether it matches the active valid preview key before calling `previewGridMove`. Preserve the existing invalid-preview handling and ensure keys still distinguish candidate/invalid target eligibility. A larger optimization would remove repeated global validation only after proving the transaction operations preserve the invariants they rely on.

**Evidence and limits.** The trigger and call ordering are directly confirmed in the full source. No representative item counts, event-rate traces, CPU profile, or frame-time measurements were collected, so user-visible latency impact and priority remain unquantified. A follow-up benchmark should replay pointer movement over a large board while staying in one snapped cell and record preview call counts and frame duration before/after. Confidence: high that duplicate work occurs; medium that it is material in typical boards.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 2. Kind-level board prefetch includes items outside the selected layout
details:
**Call path and trigger.** The board route creator groups every `board.items` entry by widget kind and calls `prefetchForKind` before it resolves the viewport-selected `layoutId`. The app and bookmarks prefetchers register item data lookups for their board items. Later, `prefetchInitialWidgetData` is explicitly given the selected layout, and `useSectionItems` renders items placed in that layout. The route then dehydrates the query client into the RSC response. Consequently, app/bookmark queries may be included in the initial response for items that have no placement in the selected layout. This is a payload and server/query work opportunity; client hydration may also retain the extra query data. It is not evidence of duplicated database records or a memory leak.

Collapsed sections retain their contents and are still mounted, so filtering only to currently visible/un-collapsed widgets is not established as safe. Filtering by selected layout placement is the narrower supported projection.

**Smallest compatible fix.** Resolve `layoutId` before constructing the kind map and pass only items whose `layouts` contains that ID into `prefetchForKind`. Keep all placed items, including collapsed-section contents.

**Evidence and limits.** The ordering, item-based prefetch API, selected-layout filtering, and dehydration path are confirmed in the route and widget code. No board counts, count of out-of-layout items, serialized RSC/dehydrated payload sizes, database query time, server heap, or browser hydration memory were measured. First measure those values on boards with multiple layouts; compare query hashes and payload bytes with and without out-of-layout placements. Confidence: high that unnecessary queries can be registered where an item is absent from the chosen layout; medium on practical payload savings because snapshot restoration and query deduplication may cover some entries.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Measurement-required candidates (not promoted to findings)
details:
- **Grid editor warmup and bundle transfer.** The board header schedules a dynamic import warmup after board load for users with edit access, with further pointer/focus warmup. This trades edit-entry latency for transferring and retaining the editor module for eligible users who may never edit. The editor boundary itself only mounts in edit mode. No production chunk sizes, network transfer, cache hit rate, or edit-use frequency were checked, so this is a bundle/latency tradeoff, not a RAM finding. Measure chunk bytes and session edit-entry rate before changing the warmup policy.
- **Backup restore peak memory.** The user-triggered restore path accepts archives up to 256 MiB, reads the archive into an `ArrayBuffer`, decompresses the database member into a `Uint8Array`, and opens it in the SQLite/WASM database. These buffers and the opened DB can overlap in lifetime, producing transient client memory pressure for large backups. Cleanup closes the temporary DB and clears its ref; no persistent leak was found. No peak-memory measurements or representative archive sizes were available. Streaming extraction or changing the accepted size is not recommended without data because it changes a supported restore path.
- **Board layout thumbnail work.** Thumbnail generation does repeated item/placement lookup while rendering a preview, and is used in board/layout selection surfaces. It is user-triggered and bounded by board size; no supported maximum or timing evidence establishes a bottleneck. Benchmark only if realistic large boards show slow switcher/settings rendering.

title: Finding: collapsed BoardCard panels retain unused duplicate-form trees
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `/manage/boards` calls `api.board.getManageOverview()` and renders one `BoardCard` per accessible board. Each card wraps `DuplicateBoardForm` in a collapsed Mantine `Collapse`, including when the user lacks `board-create`. The installed Mantine 9.6.0 implementation defaults `keepMounted` to true and wraps retained children in hidden React Activity. The baseline retains each form's DOM and creates an unobserved pending `board.exists` query-cache entry while collapsed.

**Measured behavior:** The nine-pair run found zero hidden requests in both baseline and candidate, at every card count and permission level; the suspected eager-query/network claim is rejected. Baseline hidden queries had zero observers, consistent with Activity pausing effects. At initial collapsed render, 25-card DOM was 1,122 baseline vs 647 candidate, and 100-card DOM was 4,422 vs 2,522. Initial after-GC heap median at 100 cards was 58,231,628 bytes baseline vs 52,082,400 candidate with create permission, and 58,181,380 vs 52,036,864 without. The paired candidate heap deltas were -6,152,976 bytes (range -9,157,192 to -6,128,264) and -6,143,732 bytes (range -9,148,628 to -6,126,128), respectively. These are whole-fixture totals, not per-card costs. Full calibration and formal paired details are in [board-card-browser-calibration.md](../measurements/board-card-browser-calibration.md) and [board-card-browser-pairs-9.json](../measurements/board-card-browser-pairs-9.json).

**Dimensions:** The confirmed benefit is client DOM, retained client heap, and unused pending query-cache records. Server RAM, database reads, CPU, compressed transfer, and route bundle are unchanged/unmeasured: the browser fixture saw no hidden requests, and the prop does not add data or imports. Baseline hidden trees are mounted/retained rather than repeatedly allocated after each collapse. Candidate defers allocating the form tree until opened; after opening, normal form and availability-query allocation still occurs. Query entries for actually opened names remain cached under the five-minute gcTime during the bounded run.

**Minimal compatible fix applied:** Set `keepMounted={false}` on the existing BoardCard `Collapse`. This uses Mantine's built-in lifecycle behavior and keeps the same transition path. Baseline `duplicateFormKey` increments on every reopen, so an edited draft already resets to the source board name; the nine-pair run confirmed this along with existing-name validation, available-name feedback, submit state, and exactly one mutation. At 100 cards, first-open medians were 120.9 ms baseline and 148.3 ms candidate, but paired candidate-minus-baseline median was -1.9 ms with a -64.6 to +56 ms range; no consistent latency penalty was measured. Transition timing remained `height 200ms, opacity 200ms`; some in-animation height samples differed by 2px, and post-navigation DOM snapshots were too early to establish a steady baseline plateau.

**Confidence and limits:** Confidence is high that the built-in lifecycle removes collapsed form DOM and query-cache records in this fixture; confidence in real installation memory savings is medium because the isolated fixture mocks unrelated route pieces and does not measure a full Next.js production route. Compressed network bytes, server memory, and bundle size are outside this finding because no hidden request existed and the source delta adds no data or dependency.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: group overview sends every membership record to a client that displays at most five avatars
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `/manage/users/groups` calls `api.group.getAll()` and passes its result through `GroupsList` to `GroupsTable`. The owning `group.getAll` procedure loads every group's complete `members` relation and selects each user's id, name, email, and image. The catalog uses ids/names/positions for sorting and filtering. Each row passes the full member array to `UserAvatarGroup`, which renders `users.slice(0, 5)` and only reads the total array length for the `+N` badge.

**Needed data:** The first five users need name/image and possibly email for configured Gravatar behavior. Remaining entries are only needed as a count. The current client payload therefore grows with all memberships, including email and user objects for members six onward. `group.getAll` has only this assigned route caller, so a specialized overview shape can be made without changing other in-repository callers.

**Dimensions:** Server-side database materialization and mapping currently scale with all membership rows. The full nested relation is serialized to the client and retained in the group query props/state, so transferred payload and client heap also scale with total memberships. Mapping and slicing are O(M) in total membership count; no large-list CPU measurements exist. This is excess payload/state, not an identified lifecycle leak. The effect is likely modest for small installations and can become material for large groups or many memberships.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Make the overview return only the avatar preview fields for up to five users and an aggregate member count; adapt `UserAvatarGroup` or this caller to consume `{ previewUsers, memberCount }`. A SQL-side count plus bounded related-user query is needed to reduce server materialization too; merely slicing after `findMany` would reduce transfer/retention but retain full server allocation. Preserve email only for preview users if Gravatar is enabled.

**Baseline measurement and tradeoffs:** Seed representative groups with increasing membership counts and compare server result bytes/heap, serialized RSC payload bytes, and browser retained heap after load. Keep count and avatar order identical. Confidence is high for unnecessary client fields and rows; practical impact is medium/low until real membership distributions are known. Query-shape complexity is moderate because the count and first-five preview need database support.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: hidden existing-app selector fetches the full selectable app catalog
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `/manage/integrations/new?kind=...` renders `NewIntegrationForm`. For users with `integration-create` but without `app-create`, `hasApp` starts false and the app linking section is collapsed. `AppForm` still mounts `IntegrationAppSelect`, whose `clientApi.app.selectable.useQuery()` has no `enabled` condition. `app.selectable` returns every app with id, name, icon URL, destination URL, ping URL, and description. These options are only displayed when the user enables app linking to an existing app.

**Dimensions:** This eagerly performs a request and retains all selectable app records in the client query cache, so network bytes and client heap scale with app catalog size. Server work is one full catalog query per new-integration form mount. The existing-app selector genuinely needs the option list when opened; the avoidable portion is fetching it before the control is shown. No bundle size issue is claimed because the data is runtime-loaded. No app-count or payload measurement is available.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Pass an `enabled` condition to `IntegrationAppSelect` based on `hasApp` and existing-app mode, and preserve the query cache once loaded. With `app-create`, the initial mode is new-app entry; the list is only needed after the user selects existing. Without `app-create`, it is only needed after enabling linking.

**Baseline measurement and tradeoffs:** Compare the initial request count and response bytes on the new integration route across both permission states, then enable the relevant selector and confirm options still load. The selector may briefly show its existing loader on first open. Confidence is high in the eager-fetch path and medium in impact, dependent on app count.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 1. About page mounts all contributor image tags under collapsed panels
details: `/manage/about` imports GitHub contributors, Open Collective sponsors, and translators and maps every record to `GenericContributorLinkCard` within four accordion panels (`apps/nextjs/src/app/[locale]/manage/about/page.tsx`). Local source assets contain 151 GitHub contributors, 39 sponsors, and 287 translators: 477 Avatar image elements total, backed by 62,664 bytes of JSON. The `Avatar` is passed each remote image URL without `imageProps.loading="lazy"`. The installed Mantine 9.6 implementation was inspected: Accordion panels inherit `keepMounted`; Collapse defaults to `keepMounted: true` and uses React Activity hidden mode. Thus closed panels retain/render their children, and the Avatar implementation emits a plain `` with the source URL. The user opens the About route with only the contributors panel selected, yet the other panel images are still present in mounted hidden content and can be fetched eagerly. This makes one page visit trigger up to 477 third-party image requests and creates all card/avatar UI nodes before the user opens those sections. **Dimensions:** DOM/component allocation is O(G), where G is the contributor count (currently 477); potential external transfer is the sum of remote avatar responses, which was not measured. The 62,664-byte JSON figure is the raw local source size, not compressed transfer or browser RAM. No browser network trace or heap snapshot was collected, so actual response bytes, cache hits, decode memory, and timing remain unknown. **Smallest compatible fix:** mark these Avatar images lazy, or mount contributor panel contents only after activation. Lazy image loading is the narrower change and preserves the current accordion interaction. To validate, compare a cold-cache browser network trace before/after opening `/manage/about`; record initial avatar requests and transferred bytes, then inspect decoded image memory after opening each panel. **Confidence:** medium-high for all records being rendered and the absent lazy attribute; medium for the exact number fetched immediately because browser scheduling/cache policy was not measured.

title: 2. Docker table creates four mutation observers per container row
details:
`/manage/tools/docker/page.tsx` fetches the complete Docker inventory and passes it as `initialData` into `DockerTable`. The table disables pagination and does not enable row virtualization. Its `renderRowActions` creates a `ContainerRowMenu` for each row (`docker-table.tsx`). Each menu calls `useContainerAction` four times, once each for start, stop, restart, and remove, so N visible containers create four idle TanStack mutation observers per row even though only one action is invoked for a row at a time. The action bar also owns four mutation hooks when selection actions are rendered.

This is an avoidable client-side allocation and observer subscription count of O(4N); these hooks do not retain completed mutation results for every container, so the evidence supports per-row observer/React-query state allocation rather than a claim of unbounded mutation-cache retention. Container cardinality is environment-dependent and was not collected, so absolute heap cost and render latency are unknown.

The same module's `showContainerActionResult` filters failures, then finds the matching container by scanning the container list for each failed result. For bulk actions with F failures and C selected containers, the lookup is O(F*C), worst-case O(C²). Action requests cap selected targets at 100 in `packages/api/src/router/docker/docker-router.ts`; that bounds this particular CPU path, though it can still perform up to 10,000 comparisons.

**Smallest compatible fix:** hoist the four operation mutation hooks to `DockerTable` and pass action callbacks into row menus, preserving operation-specific notifications and invalidation. For the lookup, build a `Map` keyed by endpoint ID plus container ID once per result handler. This reduces observers to a constant count and name resolution to O(F+C).

**Dimensions:** observer count scales linearly with inventory rows; the failure-name loop scales quadratically with a selected bulk operation. No React profiler, heap snapshot, representative container inventory, or mutation timing was collected. These are source-derived operation counts, not measured milliseconds or bytes.

**Confidence:** high for the hook count and nested scan; medium for material user impact because a typical configured Docker inventory size was not measured.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 3. Kubernetes service and ingress child keys change on every render
details:
`ingresses-table.tsx` calls `createId()` for every nested ingress path child, and `services-table.tsx` does the same for each service port and target port. `createId` is re-exported from `@paralleldrive/cuid2` (`packages/common/src/id.ts`), so the keys are newly generated on every cell render instead of identifying the corresponding path or port. Any table rerender therefore replaces those nested DOM children and allocates new IDs, even when the resource data is unchanged. Table search/state changes and query updates are concrete rerender triggers.

**Dimensions:** O(P) new identifiers and child replacements on a render, where P is the number of displayed nested paths/ports. This creates transient allocation and DOM/React reconciliation work, not persistent record retention. Cluster resource and nested path cardinalities were not measured; no browser profiler or mutation count was collected.

**Smallest compatible fix:** use a stable key derived from the resource identity and nested value, with an index only if duplicate values within a resource are valid. Validate with a profiler while changing the table search and confirm unchanged path/port nodes are not remounted.

**Confidence:** high that keys are unstable and cause replacement; medium for meaningful impact at typical cluster sizes.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Candidate: stale assistant focus pointer after surface unmount
details:
- **Files and trigger:** `apps/nextjs/src/components/assistant/assistant-runtime-provider.tsx`, called through `assistant-widget.tsx`. `AssistantComposerSurfaceBoundary` captures focused elements in module-level `lastFocusedSurfaceElement`; unmount removes the surface from `surfaceElements` but leaves this global unchanged when it points inside that surface.
- **Baseline evidence:** after forced GC at 1, 10, and 50 focus/unmount cycles, the global referenced a detached `TEXTAREA`; at 50 cycles 49 of 50 weak references were collected. A heap snapshot also showed browser/React-associated edges to the target. This confirms the stale module reference, but does not establish that it is the only strong retainer.
- **Prototype and rejection:** a temporary four-line cleanup checked `element.contains(lastFocusedSurfaceElement)`, then nulled the reference and reset `lastFocusedSurfaceAt`. The exact patch is archived at `audit-evidence/2026-10-11/rejected-prototypes/assistant-focus-reference-cleanup.patch`; production source has been restored. Across nine isolated baseline/live pairs, the updated source cleared the module reference every time, but both versions had 38 DOM nodes and one surviving target weak reference at 50 cycles. Median post-GC CDP `JSHeapUsedSize` was 5,436,912 bytes baseline vs 5,437,688 bytes updated; paired deltas were +32 to +1,544 bytes for live. No heap or node benefit was measured.
- **Retainer caveat and assessment:** a matched neutral render then focused an outside-assistant button, confirming that `document.activeElement` moved to the button in both modes; still one target weak reference survived in both. Snapshot paths showed a browser/React-associated edge after clearing the module global, and the narrow snapshot object-ID lookup could not attribute retained bytes. The 512 KiB sentinel is synthetic calibration, not a production-size estimate. This remains a lifecycle candidate only, not a retained-performance finding; the prototype is rejected under the audit's evidence threshold.

title: 1. Bound peak memory during SQLite restore
details:
**Files and call path:** `apps/nextjs/src/app/api/backup/import/route.ts` is called by `DatabaseRestoreFlow` at `apps/nextjs/src/components/backup/database-restore-flow.tsx:201`, available from the initialization flow and management backup UI. Admin or onboarding-claim restore is an explicit user action.

**Trigger and cause:** For an upload near the 256 MiB compressed limit, `readBoundedRequestBodyAsync` retains chunks and then allocates a contiguous body. `parseBoundedFormDataAsync` builds a `Response` and parses multipart from that body. The handler then materializes `file.arrayBuffer()`, constructs AdmZip, and `getData()` inflates the SQLite entry (allowed up to 512 MiB) before `writeFileSync`. These representations may overlap. The limits protect disk/zip-bomb bounds but do not establish a safe peak-RAM bound.

**Dimensions:** This is transient server RSS/heap and allocation pressure during restore. It does not affect browser transfer size beyond the user-uploaded archive, JS bundle size, or steady-state retention after the handler returns. No peak RSS/heap measurement or representative compressed/uncompressed fixtures were available, so the actual peak and overlap are unknown. A reasonable baseline is a controlled restore of representative and near-limit archives while recording process RSS and heap by stage; record compressed bytes and uncompressed DB bytes separately.

**Smallest compatible direction:** Stream the multipart file to a temporary file and extract the DB entry to disk through a streaming ZIP reader, retaining the existing compressed/uncompressed limits and path validation. Confirm the selected parser's ZIP64, malformed archive, duplicate entry, and traversal behavior before replacing AdmZip. This is moderate-to-high complexity and changes a security-sensitive restore path; temp-file cleanup and migration/re-encryption ordering must remain intact. Confidence: high that several large buffers are materialized in sequence; medium that they overlap enough to cause user-visible pressure; magnitude unmeasured.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 2. Avoid serializing full branding into client provider props
details:
**Files and call path:** `apps/nextjs/src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx` fetches server settings for every localized page. It passes all `serverSettings.branding` to both `SettingsProvider` and `CustomMantineProvider`, and separately emits `branding.customCss` in the root `<style>`. `CustomMantineProvider` (`_client-providers/mantine.tsx`) reads only `primaryColor`, `secondaryColor`, and `defaultRadius`. Server settings permit `customCss` up to 16,384 characters. The settings context type includes branding, but no client `useSettings().branding` consumer was found in the assigned app/package search; a broader repository consumer check is needed before removing it.

**Trigger and cause:** Every RSC render/navigation through the locale layout can carry provider props. At maximum CSS size, the same CSS may be serialized as client settings data and as Mantine provider branding in addition to the inline style. RSC may deduplicate/reference repeated values, so the duplication factor is not established from source alone.

**Dimensions:** Potential extra serialized response bytes and per-request serialization/allocation only. This does not imply extra JS bundle bytes or long-lived client RAM after parsing. No RSC capture or encoded byte measurement was available. Measure a locale route with empty CSS and a 16,384-character CSS value, compare raw Flight response bytes and server RSS/heap, and inspect whether repeated values are encoded once or multiple times.

**Smallest compatible direction:** Pass a three-field projection to `CustomMantineProvider`; if complete repository search confirms no client consumer, omit `customCss` (or branding entirely) from the client settings context while keeping the server-rendered inline style. This adds small type plumbing and could affect future settings consumers, so preserve the server layout's CSS/style behavior and verify all package consumers. Confidence: medium that the Mantine prop is over-broad; low-to-medium that it causes material wire/RAM overhead until measured.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 1. Do not retain unsupported countdown time zones indefinitely
details:
**Files and call path:** [countdown/recurrence.ts](../../../packages/widgets/src/countdown/recurrence.ts) defines a module-level `Map<string, boolean>` and caches both valid and invalid `Intl.DateTimeFormat` lookups. [countdown/component.tsx](../../../packages/widgets/src/countdown/component.tsx) calls `getCountdownEventState` for every configured event whenever the widget clock changes. The option is created in [countdown/index.ts](../../../packages/widgets/src/countdown/index.ts); [options.ts](../../../packages/widgets/src/options.ts) validates each `timeZone` as only a non-empty string and caps a widget at 20 events. The normal editor presents supported timezone choices, but the API save procedure accepts arbitrary unknown option values: `packages/api/src/router/widgets/options.ts` merges `newOptions` from a `z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())` into stored options without applying widget option schemas.

**Trigger and cause:** A board editor with modify access can save countdown events containing distinct unsupported timezone strings through the option-save API. When a mounted countdown evaluates those events, each distinct string is inserted into the process-wide map and remains there after the widget unmounts or the option changes. Repeating this with unique values grows retained entries without a bound. The normal UI does not generate this input, so this is a malformed or direct-API configuration path.

**Dimensions and complexity:** This is process-lifetime retained server/client module memory, depending on which runtime evaluates the recurrence module; the widget runs client-side, so browser heap is directly relevant. Retained memory is O(U) in the number and total length of distinct invalid timezone strings seen by that module instance. The lookup itself is O(1) after insertion. No heap measurement or proof of API request size limits was collected; material impact depends on repeated unique values and is not established.

**Smallest compatible direction:** Cache only successful timezone validations, or cap the map with a small LRU. Not caching failures avoids retaining arbitrary invalid strings while keeping the finite set of ordinary timezone values fast. This repeats the relatively cheap validation for malformed values; a bounded cache adds a little implementation complexity. Preserve the current unsupported-zone behavior.

**Confidence and gaps:** High confidence in the unbounded retention path and accepted input shape; low-to-medium confidence in user-visible impact because the supported editor does not produce invalid values and heap growth was not measured. A baseline should save/mount a controlled series of unique invalid timezone strings, record cache entry count and browser heap before/after, then verify reclamation or a stable cap after unmount/update.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 2. Avoid repeatedly copying Tracearr dashboard arrays while merging integrations
details:
**Files and call path:** [tracearr/component.tsx](../../../packages/widgets/src/tracearr/component.tsx) queries `widget.tracearr.getDashboard` and folds successful responses into `combinedData`. Each fold creates fresh arrays for accumulated `streams.data`, `streams.summary.byServer`, `violations.data`, and `recentActivity.data` with spread concatenation. The router in `packages/api/src/router/widgets/tracearr.ts` loads every selected integration through `settleIntegrationQueries`; `packages/definitions/src/widget-integration-map.ts` gives Tracearr no `maxIntegrations`. The integration's `getStreamsAsync` in `packages/integrations/src/tracearr/tracearr-integration.ts` parses the upstream streams array without a page-size parameter or local cap. The widget refreshes every 10 seconds.

**Trigger and cause:** With multiple selected Tracearr integrations returning many active sessions, each reduce step recopies all previously accumulated rows. For equally sized responses, the merge work grows quadratically with integration count for each merged array, instead of linearly with total rows. The component also maps streams into sourced display rows; that copy is needed to attach integration labels/keys and is separate from the repeated prefix copies.

**Dimensions and complexity:** This is transient client CPU and allocation churn during each query update, with temporary arrays proportional to accumulated response size. It is not evidence of a retained-memory leak. The transfer is the upstream response size and is unaffected by the local merge. No real response sizes, browser CPU profile, or peak heap comparison were available, so the user-visible cost is unknown.

**Smallest compatible direction:** Build the aggregate with local mutable arrays and append each integration's rows once, or precompute per-field results in a single pass. This keeps source arrays untouched and makes merge work O(total rows); it trades a purely functional reducer for a locally mutated accumulator. Keep summary values and partial-integration behavior identical.

**Confidence and gaps:** High confidence in the repeated-copy complexity and unbounded integration selection; medium confidence that it is material in practice. Measure browser CPU and heap for one versus several integrations with representative and stress-sized stream responses, and record response bytes/rows. There is no production change or benchmark in this audit.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 1. RSS compact mode eagerly loads an image for every feed entry
details:
`packages/widgets/src/rssFeed/component.tsx` calls `getFeeds` with `maximumAmountPosts` from the widget options, defaulting to 100. The compact branch maps every returned entry. For every entry with an enclosure it renders a background `Image` without `loading="lazy"` (lines 180–196), regardless of the `showPosterImage` option. The optional foreground poster is a second image and does use lazy loading (lines 198–208). The definition permits up to 9,999 posts (`packages/widgets/src/rssFeed/index.ts`, lines 47–50); the API accepts up to 100 feed URLs and requests `count` entries from each, then globally slices to `maximumAmountPosts` (`packages/api/src/router/widgets/rssFeed.ts`). Thus a single widget can return and render up to 9,999 compact entries, each potentially causing an offscreen enclosure image request. With `showPosterImage` enabled, a card may create two image elements for the same enclosure.

**Dimensions and cause:** React/DOM and image-element allocation scales with returned entries. Eager image requests can increase image transfer, decode work, and decoded-image memory while the scroll area is mounted. The feed JSON response and React Query cache also retain the entry records; that is a separate payload/cache dimension. The output cap is a hard maximum but still much higher than a typical visible compact list. These are source-derived upper bounds, not observed requests or memory.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Set `loading="lazy"` on the background image. Consider rendering it only when the visual option is enabled, after checking whether the background is intended to be independent of the poster option. Preserve the configured entry count unless product behavior calls for a lower cap.

**Compatibility and tradeoffs:** Native lazy loading preserves scroll content and option behavior, while delaying images until near the viewport. Suppressing the background when `showPosterImage` is false changes current compact-mode appearance and needs a product decision. A lower entry cap would also change visible behavior for users who intentionally configured large feeds.

**Evidence and gaps:** Source cap and render cardinality were inspected; no browser network trace, response-size measurement, compressed-transfer measurement, decoded-image memory measurement, or React profile was collected. Validate with a cold-cache dashboard containing a large feed, recording image requests before and while scrolling, plus the serialized query response separately from transferred/compressed bytes.

title: 2. Media request cards eagerly load poster and original-size backdrop images
details:
`packages/widgets/src/media-requests/list/component.tsx` maps all returned requests to cards (lines 77–86). Each card emits a backdrop `Image` with no lazy-loading prop (lines 131–141), and emits another poster `Image` for non-tiny layouts, also without lazy loading (lines 151–161). The Overseerr integration fetches up to 20 pending and 20 recently modified requests, then de-duplicates pending entries; therefore it returns at most 40 records per integration for this path (`packages/integrations/src/overseerr/overseerr-integration.ts`). The backdrop URL uses TMDB's `/original/` image size, while the poster requests a 600-by-900 rendition. A board may select multiple integrations, multiplying the returned cards and image tags.

**Dimensions and cause:** Card and image-element allocation grows with returned records. Images below the visible portion of the scroll area are not explicitly lazy, so the browser may request/decode them before the user scrolls to the cards. The original backdrop size can make transfer/decode cost materially higher than a small thumbnail, but no size or actual request measurement is available. This does not establish long-lived JS retention; it is potential transfer, decode, and transient decoded-image memory.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Add `loading="lazy"` to both card images. If the image provider supports a suitable backdrop thumbnail URL, use that for the background while preserving a larger poster where the UI needs it.

**Compatibility and tradeoffs:** Lazy loading retains the current card appearance as items approach the viewport. Changing the backdrop rendition may alter image quality and depends on the integration's URL contract; implement it only with provider support.

**Evidence and gaps:** The card render path, image URLs, and per-integration request cap were inspected. No configured integration count, browser network trace, actual asset byte size, compressed transfer, or decoded-image memory was measured. Validate on a board with multiple integrations and a cold image cache; compare request count/bytes before and after scrolling.

**Confidence:** High on the eager image tags and 40-record per-integration upper bound; medium on user impact and actual transfer due to unknown integration counts, caching, and browser scheduling.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 3. Archive Team Warrior sends and caches item details even for compact widgets
details:
`packages/widgets/src/archive-team-warrior/component.tsx` uses a suspense query for `getStatus` and always receives `data.status`. Compact display reads project/status/count/bandwidth fields, while only advanced display consumes and maps `status.items` into individual cards (lines 53–65 and 104–170). The server status handler builds a status snapshot containing the item map and returns the full status object. The query consumer therefore receives and caches item details for compact widgets that do not render them. The common request-handler cache can retain returned results; each load makes a fresh status snapshot, so the observation is per-response/query retention, not an accumulating map across refreshes.

**Dimensions and cause:** Response serialization and network transfer scale with item count and item-field lengths. React Query cache retains the complete response while the query remains cached. In compact mode, there is no corresponding item-card DOM allocation, but the records still occupy response/cache memory. No item-count cap or payload projection is visible in this widget call path.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Provide a compact status projection that excludes `items`, or make item details an advanced-only query. Keep summary counts and status fields identical. Confirm cache keys and invalidation remain separated so compact and advanced queries cannot reuse incompatible shapes.

**Compatibility and tradeoffs:** Splitting/projection reduces compact payload and cached data but adds a query/API contract and could increase request count when switching to advanced mode. If current item lists are small, added complexity may outweigh savings.

**Evidence and gaps:** Full response construction, query use, and compact/advanced rendering were inspected. No item-count distribution, serialized payload size, compressed transfer, cache occupancy, RSS, or user-visible latency was measured. Validate compact and advanced modes against small and large snapshots, measuring response bytes and cache size independently.

**Confidence:** High that compact mode does not use the item details while receiving the full response; medium-low that this is material because typical item count and serialized size are unknown.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 4. Compact weather statically imports the chart-only advanced subtree
details:
`packages/widgets/src/weather/component.tsx` statically imports both `AdvancedWeather` and `CompactWeather` and chooses between them at render time. `weather/advanced.tsx` imports `CompositeChart` from `@mantine/charts`, while compact mode does not render that subtree. The outer widget definition dynamically loads the entire widget component, so this is not an eager import on every dashboard; it means the weather widget chunk can include the advanced chart dependency even when a user only uses compact mode.

**Dimensions and cause:** Potential client bundle bytes and transfer increase for compact-only weather users. The statically imported chart subtree is also evaluated as part of the widget chunk; the source does not establish a persistent RAM increase attributable to it. No built chunk or compressed network size was measured.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Split `AdvancedWeather` with a dynamic import or a separate lazy boundary selected only for advanced mode. Keep the current outer widget-level lazy loading.

**Compatibility and tradeoffs:** The advanced view may incur an additional chunk request and brief loading state the first time it opens. A split only helps if the production bundler emits a distinct chunk and compact-only routes do not preload it.

**Evidence and gaps:** Static import graph was inspected. No bundle analyzer output, generated chunk mapping, transfer-size report, parse/evaluation timing, or heap measurement was collected. Validate with production build analyzer/network data for a dashboard containing compact weather only and one using advanced weather.

**Confidence:** High that source statically imports the advanced chart graph; medium that it increases delivered bundle bytes because actual chunking and tree shaking were not measured.

title: Finding: Stocks builds an unused full-size graph array in advanced display
details:
**Call path and trigger:** The stock widget is lazily loaded by its definition. On any successful `getPriceHistory` result, `StockPriceWidget` calls `getStockSummary`; this happens for both compact and advanced display modes.

**Evidence and cause:** `getStockSummary` computes `graphValues` with `priceHistory.map(...)`, but the advanced branch renders `Sparkline` from `data.priceHistory` directly and never reads `summary.graphValues`. The array is therefore created and kept in the render-local summary until that render completes, then becomes collectible. It is a transient duplicate, not a leak. `Math.min(...priceHistory)` and `Math.max(...priceHistory)` also spread every observation into function arguments. The widget exposes ranges through `max` and intervals through `5m`, but this audit did not trace or measure an upper bound on provider response length.

**Dimensions and evidence gaps:** For N observations, the extra advanced-mode mapping is O(N) CPU and O(N) transient number storage. The min/max calls are O(N); large arrays may encounter JavaScript argument-count limits, but no response large enough to reproduce that behavior was measured. No latency, heap, or API response-size measurement is available, so practical impact is unquantified.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Pass display mode into summary construction or move graph normalization into the compact-only render path, so advanced mode does not build `graphValues`. Replace spread-based min/max with a single loop to avoid argument expansion while preserving O(N) work. Keep the source query array unchanged for the advanced Sparkline. This saves one O(N) pass and temporary array in advanced mode; the compact chart still needs its normalized series. Confidence is medium for the unnecessary advanced allocation and low-to-medium for user-visible impact pending real history-size measurements.

title: Finding: successful query cache retained parsed responses after expiry while idle
details:
**Call path and trigger.** `packages/api/src/router/custom-widget/preview-query-procedures.ts` builds a `custom-jsx:preview:<session>:<request>:<params>:<connection-version>` key and passes `request.cacheSeconds` to `executeCustomWidgetRequest`. `packages/api/src/router/custom-widget/management-queries.ts` does the same for option queries with a 30-second default. On a successful cacheable query, `packages/custom-widgets/src/server/request-executor.ts` stores the already parsed and redacted response object in the module-level `cache` map. Request schema allows `cacheSeconds` through 3600 seconds.

**Cause and measured evidence.** Before the fix, the cache held at most 1,000 entries and expired entries were reclaimed only on later insertions or matching-key lookups. A 1-second TTL followed by 100 ms idle left parsed responses in the cache until explicit invalidation or another insertion. In nine alternating fresh-process pairs using Node 24.18.0, `--max-old-space-size=512`, and the actual executor with a loopback HTTP fixture, median 100-entry `heapUsed` after expiry was 42,070,424 bytes before versus 16,213,736 bytes after the fix. Explicit invalidation freed a median 26,246,352 bytes before the fix versus 1,296 bytes after. With 25 entries, the paired idle heap reduction was 6,549,552 bytes. The fixture sent 25 or 100 requests concurrently via `Promise.all`; each response contained a 262,144-byte payload string and a 262,172-byte serialized JSON body. This is controlled fixture evidence, not a claim about typical production response sizes. The 1 MiB input response limit and entry cap are not an aggregate memory budget.

**Dimensions and limits.** Five repeated 25-entry expiry cycles showed baseline idle heap plateauing around 22.50 MB rather than growing per cycle; the existing next-insertion prune reclaimed the preceding expired batch. The bug is bounded stale retention during idle by the existing 1,000-entry cap, not an unbounded leak. Measurements include the fixture server and executor in one Node process. Per-process sampled maximum RSS medians were 215,764,992 bytes baseline and 219,398,144 bytes after, with overlapping ranges; this does not establish an RSS improvement or a process peak. The result supports heap reclamation only. There is no client bundle or network-transfer cost from this server cache.

**Smallest compatible fix.** Implemented one unref'd timer for the earliest cache expiry in `request-executor.ts`. Insertions compare the new deadline in O(1); when the timer fires, it prunes expired entries and scans for the next deadline in O(C), with C bounded by the existing cap. The callback does not run capacity eviction, capture response values, or change cache epochs/in-flight requests. Long finite TTLs are clamped to Node's 2,147,483,647 ms timer limit and rescheduled. The existing entry cap and request/cache semantics remain in place.

**Tradeoffs and validation.** The timer adds one unref'd handle and an O(C) expiry cleanup/next-deadline scan, at most once per expiry batch; partial invalidation can cause a harmless early timer wake. Idle-window process CPU measurements were noisy (100-entry median 1.31 ms baseline versus 7.53 ms after over the 1.1-second wait), so they do not isolate callback cost; the expected bounded scan cost is explicit. All 18 paired runs passed cache-hit, expiry-refetch, refreshed-hit, and in-flight generation assertions. Separate baseline and fixed runs each inserted 1,001 unique keys and verified oldest-entry eviction. Raw samples, runtime/source hashes, controls, and limitations are in `audit-evidence/2026-10-11/measurements/cache-expiry-results.md` and its adjacent JSONL files. No production-distribution or maximum-size workload was measured.

**Confidence and gaps.** High that the pre-fix cache retained expired parsed responses under idle conditions and that the timer reclaims them in the measured fixture. Real-world impact depends on response sizes and cache activity; production payload distributions were not measured. The cache stores already-redacted response data; the fix does not alter the credential-redaction boundary or cache keys.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding F1: every bound input edit re-copies and serializes the full response graph
details:
**Call path and trigger.** `CustomJsxDisplay` in `packages/widgets/src/custom-api/custom-jsx-display.tsx` passes the widget data and `SAFE_BINDINGS` (`createCustomJsxBindings`) into `CustomJsxRenderer`. A bound control calls `setInputValue` in `runtime-components.tsx`, which replaces input state and rerenders `CustomJsxRendererSession`. Its `useMemo` depends on `inputs`; each value edit therefore calls `createBindings(data)`, runs the JSX interpreter again, and calls `createBoundaryKey(template, bindings)`. The key helper currently does `JSON.stringify(bindings)` before hashing the string (`runtime/custom-jsx-renderer.tsx`, lines 188-204 and 266-271; see also `runtime-components.tsx` lines 95-155 and `widgets/src/custom-api/custom-jsx-display.tsx` lines 70-83).

**Cause and impact.** `createCustomJsxBindings` sanitizes by traversing and copying the response tree (`jsx/bindings.ts`, lines 4-8 and 16-82). The backend accepts response bodies up to 1 MiB and JSON structures up to 50,000 nodes (`server/response.ts`, lines 6-8 and 24-50). For a response with `N` nodes and `B` serialized bytes, each input edit causes another O(N) sanitize/copy and O(B) serialization, in addition to the needed template parse/evaluation. The sanitized copy and `JSON.stringify` result are temporary allocations; `createBoundaryKey` retains only the short hash string, so this is repeated CPU and peak temporary memory, not cumulative retained growth. Frequent text input edits make the repeated work especially visible. Current limits bound one pass but do not amortize it across edits.

**Smallest compatible fix.** Build the boundary key from the template, identity/version tokens for the original data/status/options objects, and an input-state revision (or a small input-only fingerprint). This preserves boundary reset behavior when the template, request data, options, status, or bound values change without serializing the sanitized response graph. Keep the sanitized copy for interpreter safety and rendering.

**Tradeoffs and confidence.** A monotonic input revision is O(1) but resets the error boundary on every value change, which is consistent with the current key changing for every changed input. Stable object identity tokens avoid stringifying large data/status/options and preserve upstream-change resets. Confidence: high for the repeated traversal/serialization path; the visible latency and peak heap impact are unmeasured.

**Evidence still needed.** Profile the production widget renderer with a near-limit response and a text-bound input. Compare per-keystroke scripting time and peak heap before/after, recording response bytes/node count and input edit count. No browser profile or benchmark was run in this audit.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: 1. Integration middleware loads full nested item rows for a board access check
details:
**Call path and trigger.** Any API procedure composed with `createOneIntegrationMiddleware*` or `createManyIntegrationMiddleware*` enters the corresponding factory in `packages/api/src/middlewares/integration.ts`. The database query requests `items: { with: { item: true } }`, loading each linked integration-item association and every field of its `item` row. The relation is destructured as `_ignore1` before `next()`, but it is not dead: `hasQueryAccessToIntegrationsAsync` in `packages/auth/permissions/integration-query-permissions.ts` reads `integration.items[].item.boardId` to enforce board-inherited query access. The factories are used by integration and widget query/action procedures throughout `packages/api/src/router/` (for example, calendar, downloads, and media server).

**Cost and dimensions.** For one integration, the avoidable work grows with the number of linked item associations; for the many-integration path it grows with the sum of associations for all requested integrations. This adds database result materialization and transfer to the API process, transient server RAM, and ORM/object construction CPU. It does not increase the final tRPC response or network payload because the relation is discarded before the procedure handler returns. The supplied pre-change source-measurement baseline used 250 linked items with 32 KiB option data each: materialized query result size was 8,243,961 bytes and held post-GC heap delta was 8,276,016 bytes. These are database-query-result and in-process heap measurements, not HTTP/tRPC network bytes. The main dashboard schema permits many items per board, so this relation is not structurally capped by this middleware.

**Cause and smallest fix.** The nested item projection included all columns even though access checks consume only `item.boardId`. Implemented: all three matching nested item relation projections in `middlewares/integration.ts` (one- and many-integration factories) and `router/integration/integration-router.ts` now select only `boardId`, retaining the association rows. App, secrets, user permissions, and group permissions remain as before. The selection change preserves the `integration.items[].item.boardId` auth contract.

**Compatibility and tradeoffs.** This does not change the tRPC input/output, authorization decision, ordering, or freshness; it narrows internal fields while retaining `boardId` for access checks. No API compatibility change is expected. The post-change paired measurement is pending the root harness; no reduction is claimed yet. Validate parity for board-inherited access and compare selected columns, database result bytes, and process heap/CPU at the same fixture. Confidence: high for avoiding unused columns; measured magnitude remains pending.

title: 2. Anonymous app visibility scans and parses all app/bookmark widgets on each lookup
details:
**Call path and trigger.** `app.byId` calls `AppRepository.getByIdAsync()`, which delegates to `getByIdsAsync()` and `AppAccessControl.canUserSeeAppsAsync()`. `app.byIds` uses the same path. For anonymous callers, `getAllAppIdsOnPublicBoardsAsync()` queries all `app` and `bookmarks` items without filtering to public boards in SQL and without projecting columns. It fetches each item row plus `board.isPublic`, filters private boards in JavaScript, parses each public item’s SuperJSON `options`, and collects app IDs. Signed-in callers bypass this scan.

**Cost and dimensions.** Each anonymous lookup performs work proportional to all app/bookmark widget rows across the instance, including private-board rows, and parses option payloads on public rows. Repeated `byId` requests repeat the scan. The avoidable dimensions are DB result transfer/materialization, transient API RAM, and SuperJSON parse CPU; no bytes leave the API from this scan itself. `byIds` has no input array maximum, but the repeated whole-table scan is independent of requested IDs and is the primary issue. No live row counts, byte counts, timings, or heap measurements were collected.

**Cause and smallest fix.** The access check needs only IDs parsed from app/bookmark options on public boards, but it loads complete item rows and performs visibility filtering afterward. Use a narrow select for `kind` and `options`, join/filter public boards in the database, and consider resolving only requested app IDs while preserving bookmark semantics. The exact query change should retain the rule that a bookmarked app counts as visible only when that bookmark widget is on a public board.

**Compatibility and tradeoffs.** Preserve the current anonymous rule, logged-in fast path, and public-board visibility. A DB-side join changes query shape but not output or authorization ordering. Verify parity for direct app widgets, bookmark widgets, private/public boards, and mixed requested IDs; measure rows and bytes read as total private and public widget counts grow. Confidence: high for repeated broad scan; workload impact is unmeasured.

title: Finding: media-search integration lookup materializes complete linked widget rows
details:
**Call path and trigger:** Spotlight's media mode first calls `integration.mediaRequestSearchTargets` and then calls `integration.searchMediaRequests` for an enabled remote media query. The targets query has a 60-second stale time; the search query is keyed by the current remote query. Both procedures call `getAccessibleMediaRequestSearchIntegrationsAsync` in `packages/api/src/router/integration/integration-router.ts` (lines 617–659 and helper lines 800–832).

**Cause and proof of need:** That helper loads `items: { with: { item: true } }` for every matching media integration. The relation is integration → integration item → item row. `hasQueryAccessToIntegrationsAsync` needs the linked rows for board-inherited integration access, but reads only `integration.items[].item.boardId` (see `packages/auth/permissions/integration-query-permissions.ts`, lines 10–23 and 30–58). The media target response projects identity, name, kind, URL and interaction permission. The search path uses integration identity/kind/URL, linked app href, secrets, and permission relations; it does not use widget item kind or serialized options. The item table also stores `options` and `advancedOptions` text (`packages/db/schema/sqlite.ts`, lines 418–426), which are included in each full related row.

**Dimensions:** For I linked widget placements across matching integrations, each request materializes O(I) association and full item records in application memory and performs corresponding DB row work. The avoidable portion includes each row's options strings; exact allocated bytes and query duration are unknown. This is DB-to-process row materialization, not client response data: the targets response is projected, and the search response contains upstream search results. No network-transfer-byte claim is made. Repeated invocation during Spotlight searches repeats the lookup, subject to query caching; no retained server-side item cache was found in this helper.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Keep the association relation and authorization flow, but project the nested item to `columns: { boardId: true }`. Keep the integration permission relations and all app/secrets data currently consumed by the search logic. This preserves the list of linked boards, including empty/non-empty membership checks, and avoids loading item options and other item fields. Confirm the selected Drizzle relation shape remains accepted by `hasQueryAccessToIntegrationsAsync` and both endpoints.

**Tradeoffs and evidence still needed:** Narrow projection adds a schema-aware query selection that must stay aligned with the auth helper's board-ID requirement. Measure with fixtures or representative production-like data containing increasing linked widget counts and large option strings: DB query duration, rows/column bytes returned by the driver, request wall time, and server heap before/after. Compare targets and search results for direct integration permission, board-inherited permission, inaccessible integration, and no linked items. The current code establishes the avoidable payload; it does not establish a material user impact. Confidence is high in the unnecessary fields and medium in impact.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: icon-picker searches rank the entire icon catalog on every query
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `IconPicker` debounces draft input by 250 ms, calls `clientApi.icon.findIcons` with `limitPerGroup: 24`, and keeps previous results as placeholder data (`packages/forms-collection/src/icon-picker/icon-picker.tsx`, lines 78–88). `findIcons` is also exposed as an MCP tool. For each non-empty term, the router reads every icon's id, name, and URL for every repository, ranks them in JavaScript, sorts matching rows, and only then slices each repository to the requested limit (`packages/api/src/router/icons.ts`, lines 17–50). Empty-term browsing is already limited in SQL.

**Dimensions:** For N catalog icons and M matches, a non-empty search reads/materializes O(N) icon rows and runs matching over O(N) candidates, followed by O(M log M) sorting and O(M) temporary match/result arrays. The return is capped at 24 rows per repository for the picker, so this finding does not claim that all icon data is sent to the browser. Actual catalog size, per-search latency, memory delta, and database driver bytes were not measured; those determine practical impact. Intermediate ranking arrays are temporary, not evidence of retained memory or a leak.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Do not apply a simple result limit before ranking, because that can change the best matches. If representative measurements justify a fix, move candidate selection to a normalized searchable DB value or equivalent indexed representation while preserving `normalizeImageName`/`getImageMatchRank` semantics, SVG tie-breaking, and per-repository limits. This likely requires extending icon ingestion/schema and should be scoped only after measuring the current catalog and query path.

**Tradeoffs and evidence still needed:** A precomputed searchable representation adds stored data and index/ingestion work; an approximate SQL predicate risks dropping valid accent-, punctuation-, extension-, token-, or prefix-based matches. First record icon row count by repository and benchmark common and adversarial searches against the existing ranking, including full result equality, query duration, temporary heap, and DB-to-process bytes. Confidence is high in the O(N) path and medium-low in user impact or fix priority without those measurements.

title: Finding: calendar feed parsing has no aggregate input or output bound
details:
**Call path and trigger:** The calendar request handler authorizes/selects an integration, computes a month range with six days of padding on either side, and invokes `ICalIntegration.getCalendarEventsAsync`. Whenever a board loads an iCal calendar, this method downloads the configured private feed.

**Evidence and cause:** `getCalendarEventsAsync` buffers the complete response as a string, parses the complete string into a jCal structure and `ICAL.Component`, retains arrays/maps for all VEVENT components and exceptions, then appends matching recurring occurrences to a result array. A 100,000-iteration limit applies independently to each recurring master; it does not bound response bytes, component count, or total occurrences across all masters. The final result array is returned to the calendar request path.

**Dimensions:** For response size B, VEVENT count C, and expanded occurrences R, the path has O(B + C + R) parsing/mapping work and O(B + C + R) peak data proportional to the raw string, parsed graph, indexes, and output. The raw string and parsed graph are concurrently live during parse/expansion. This is per request and released afterward. Network transfer is the complete feed; nothing here indicates a package-size or process-lifetime leak. No representative feed size, heap peak, or parse time was measured.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Enforce a maximum response byte count while consuming the body, and add a total per-request occurrence/component budget in addition to the current per-master guard. Return a controlled integration error when the feed exceeds the byte budget; define whether occurrence-budget exhaustion returns a partial calendar with a warning or an error. Keep the existing month range, event mapping, and per-master limit unless measurements justify changing them.

**Authorization, cache freshness, and tradeoffs:** Apply bounds inside the integration after the existing integration-selection/authorization path; this does not alter permissions or cache keys/freshness. A byte limit prevents parse amplification but rejects unusually large legitimate feeds; an aggregate occurrence limit can omit valid dense calendars if treated as partial success. Select limits from observed feed distributions before implementation. Compare old/new with representative small, large, exception-heavy, and high-frequency recurrence feeds; measure response bytes, peak heap, parse CPU, and returned event count. No such measurements are available here. Confidence is high in the unbounded source path and medium in user impact because feed-size distribution is unknown.
