title: Finding: optional SABnzbd archive history scans and materializes far beyond the returned limit
details:
**Call path and trigger:** The downloads widget sends `includeArchivedHistory` (default false), `historyWindowDays` (default 7), and `limitPerIntegration` (default 50) through the API and request handler to `SabnzbdIntegration`. When archive history is enabled, the integration requests archived pages sequentially through `getSabnzbdHistorySlotsAsync`.

**Evidence and cause:** The helper can fetch 100 pages of 100 entries (10,000 archived rows), retaining all rows in `archivedSlots`. It then constructs further arrays for active/archived data, filters, sorts all in-window completed records, deduplicates, and returns the full list. The integration maps every returned history slot, concatenates it with mapped queue slots, then slices to `input.limit`. The API input has no maximum for `limitPerIntegration`; its normal widget default is 50. Archive scanning is opt-in and has an explicit 10,000-row ceiling, so this is bounded work rather than a leak.

**Dimensions:** With N scanned rows (N ≤ 10,000), source work includes O(N) page transfer and parsing plus O(N log N) sort CPU. Several O(N) arrays/sets can coexist during selection, then all selected history rows are mapped before the final limit. The output/cache contains only the final normalized result; the request handler caches that result for 10 seconds, not the archive pages. The main avoidable cost is transient server heap and sort/mapping CPU. Transfer is still needed to find entries inside the requested time window unless the provider contract safely guarantees ordering and the scan can stop. No peak heap or provider response-size measurements were taken.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Keep the sequential page fetch and 10,000-row safety ceiling. Maintain only the most recent completed candidates needed to fill the remaining result slots while scanning, deduplicate against active history, and avoid mapping archived records that cannot be returned. Do not stop early based on presumed page ordering until that contract is verified. Validate a finite API maximum for `limitPerIntegration` separately if large limits are not a supported use case.

**Authorization, cache freshness, and tradeoffs:** Preserve the existing downloads integration middleware, archive opt-in, history-window cutoff, queue-first ordering, and 10-second cache freshness. Bounded top-K retention reduces temporary memory and sort work but does not reduce network transfer when all pages must be inspected. An early stop could reduce transfer but risks dropping newer entries if page ordering differs from assumptions. Compare identical fixtures containing duplicate IDs, active history, in-window/out-of-window rows, and a full 10,000-row scan; record response bytes, heap peak, and CPU. These measurements and verified live ordering evidence are missing. Confidence is high for the extra materialization; medium for practical impact due the explicit cap and opt-in.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: Aria2 duplicates the full result lists before applying the UI limit
details:
**Call path and trigger:** The downloads API passes `limitPerIntegration` to `Aria2Integration.getClientJobsAndStatusAsync`; the normal widget default is 50. Each call requests active, waiting, stopped, and global status concurrently.

**Evidence and cause:** `tellActive()` returns all active downloads because this API call has no limit argument. The integration then spreads all active rows plus the requested waiting/stopped pages into a new array and calls `slice(0, limit)`, creating another selected array. Only that selected array is mapped. Therefore active response transfer and parsing are provider/API constraints, while the full spread and the additional slice are avoidable.

**Dimensions:** For A active and L requested rows, the response remains O(A + L) and unavoidable. Current extra array copying is O(A + L) transient references before the O(L) slice and O(L) normalized output; mapping CPU is O(L). This is per request and does not establish long-lived retention. `limitPerIntegration` currently has no API maximum. No high-A fixture, heap profile, or CPU measurement was available.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Iterate the three response arrays in their current order and append only the first `limit` rows to one selected array, then map it. Preserve the existing ordering and `paused` calculation over the selected rows. This removes the full concatenated copy without claiming to reduce the provider response or wire transfer.

**Authorization, cache freshness, and tradeoffs:** Keep the current integration authorization path, output ordering, and 10-second downloads cache behavior. The implementation is small and behavior-preserving for positive limits; a separate limit validation change would affect API behavior and needs its own compatibility decision. Measure allocations/CPU against the same fixture with large A and ordinary L; evidence is currently missing. Confidence is high for the avoidable copy and low-to-medium for user impact because active-list sizes are unknown.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: static package barrel creates an eager import path around the lazy factory
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `packages/integrations/package.json` maps the package root to `index.ts`; that file re-exports `src/index.ts`. The source barrel statically re-exports concrete integration classes, including the assigned media clients. API routers import runtime `mockWidgetData` from the package root in many widget routers. Meanwhile, `base/creator.ts` deliberately uses explicit dynamic imports for concrete integrations so runtime tooling can create lazy chunks.

**Evidence and cause:** The source dependency graph from a runtime root import reaches the broad integration barrel and its concrete implementation exports, even when the importing router only needs mock fixture data. Under native ESM evaluation, static re-export dependencies are loaded with the barrel. Next/Turbopack may prune or split some of this graph, so this audit does not establish that all modules land in one production chunk or are evaluated in the deployed server process.

**Dimensions:** The potential dimensions are cold server module loading, initialization CPU, retained module state, and server bundle bytes. No source-size, generated chunk, startup-time, or heap measurement was taken; no package-byte or RAM reduction is claimed. This is an import-graph finding, not a demonstrated memory leak.

**Minimal compatible fix:** Export mock fixtures through a dedicated subpath and update API runtime imports to that path; move any remaining runtime constants/errors used by the API to narrow subpaths as needed. Keep root exports only where compatibility requires them, and keep concrete instance creation in the dynamic factory. Inspect generated server chunks and module evaluation before deciding whether broader public export changes are warranted.

**Authorization, cache freshness, and tradeoffs:** This does not change integration authorization or data cache semantics. The narrow subpath reduces coupling for internal runtime consumers but adds package exports and may leave external root consumers unchanged. Verify by comparing the exact production server chunk graph and cold-start module load before/after, including whether Jellyfin/Immich/ical.js/Nextcloud modules are reachable from a router importing only mocks. Until that evidence exists, confidence is medium for the static source path and low-to-medium for deployed impact.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding 1: Beszel SSE parser accepts unbounded incomplete lines and frames
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `packages/api/src/router/widgets/beszel.ts` creates the live subscription and invokes `BeszelIntegration.subscribeRealtimeMetrics`; the integration decodes stream chunks and passes them to `PocketBaseSseParser.push`. In `packages/integrations/src/beszel/pocketbase-realtime.ts:10-27,42-63`, `buffer` grows until a newline and `dataLines` grows until a blank frame delimiter. A configured Beszel endpoint that emits a very long unterminated line, or keeps sending `data:` lines without the delimiter, therefore prevents dispatch while retaining all accumulated input.

**Cause and dimensions:** Neither line nor frame has a byte/character cap. The consumer queue's four-event limit (`packages/api/src/router/widgets/beszel.ts:19,211,240`) applies only after dispatch and cannot constrain a partial frame. Parser-retained strings are O(N) in bytes received for each open subscription; decoding and string concatenation can create transient copies. This is a retained-input issue, not an inference from dependency size. The stream is intentionally long-lived, so ordinary wall-clock timeout is not a valid bound. No baseline frame sizes, heap measurements, or concurrency counts are available.

**Minimal compatible fix and constraints:** Bound line and aggregate frame bytes in `PocketBaseSseParser`; on overflow, fail that stream and use the existing abort/retry cleanup. Preserve UTF-8 chunk handling and normal event semantics. Select the limit from representative real snapshots, since too-low a cap could reject valid high-container-count snapshots. Validate raw/decoded frame distributions and peak retained parser state at one and concurrent subscriptions, then verify normal frames, split code points, oversized unterminated lines/frames, reconnect, and client abort. Confidence is high on the unbounded code path, medium on material impact.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding 2: Synology API-definition cache grows with integration ID churn
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `SynologyIntegration` obtains a client via `getClient` (`packages/integrations/src/synology/synology-integration.ts:101`); API calls resolve endpoint definitions through `packages/integrations/src/synology/synology-client.ts:353-388`. The module-level `apiDefinitionCache` at line 52 keys definitions by integration ID and API name. Successful lookups remain in the map indefinitely. The client is created through the integration factory per request (`packages/integrations/src/base/creator.ts:312-313`), while the cache outlives those clients. Deleting an integration does not clear this map: the authorized delete path in `packages/api/src/router/integration/integration-router.ts:415-438` removes database and shared response-cache state but does not call the Synology cache.

**Cause and dimensions:** For each distinct ID, only a fixed set of API definitions used by this client is reachable, and each value contains small path/version metadata. Thus growth is O(I × A), where I is the number of distinct IDs encountered during the process lifetime and A is the fixed API-name set; the cache does not retain response payloads. This is an unbounded cardinality/lifetime issue, but no runtime count or process memory measurement establishes material impact.

**Minimal compatible fix and constraints:** Add a bounded LRU/TTL or targeted invalidation on successful integration deletion, ideally with a cap as a fallback for IDs that disappear through other lifecycle paths. Keep cache lookup behavior for active integrations. Eviction may cause a later request to refetch Synology's API info endpoint; it must not change authentication ordering or cache user response data. Verify map cardinality during repeated create/use/delete churn and ensure concurrent misses do not corrupt definitions. Confidence is high on indefinite retention, low-to-medium on impact because each value is small and A is fixed.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding 3: TrueNAS integration deletion leaves reusable sockets and map entries
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `TrueNasIntegration.getClient` creates a client for requests (`packages/integrations/src/truenas/truenas-integration.ts:103-116`). `TrueNasClient` holds module-static `connectionMap` and `apiMap` keyed by integration ID (`packages/integrations/src/truenas/truenas-client.ts:36-37`). Successful connections are retained for reuse (`:69-80`); normal cleanup shown in this client is failure/server-close handling and explicit connection testing (`:56-58,98-104`). The API deletion mutation authorizes first, deletes the integration, then clears shared integration response cache (`packages/api/src/router/integration/integration-router.ts:415-438`), but does not evict these maps. Trigger: make a successful TrueNAS request, then delete the integration while its remote websocket remains open. Its socket and static entries can remain until the remote closes or the process exits.

**Cause and dimensions:** This retains a live network resource and per-ID map state, rather than merely a small metadata cache. With D deleted integrations whose peers remain open, retained connections/map entries scale O(D); active socket buffers are runtime-dependent and were not measured. The code does not establish how frequently the remote closes idle sessions, so no byte estimate or impact magnitude is claimed.

**Minimal compatible fix and constraints:** Provide an ID-scoped cleanup operation on `TrueNasClient`/a connection manager and call it only after the delete permission check and successful database deletion (alongside existing cache invalidation). Cleanup should close the socket and remove both maps, while safely handling an in-flight connection promise. An idle TTL is a useful fallback for missed lifecycle paths. Preserve reuse while an integration is active and avoid cleanup before authorization or before delete success. Verify concurrent request/delete ordering, in-flight connection settlement, and remote-close behavior; measure open sockets and map cardinality under delete churn. Confidence is high that deletion currently lacks cleanup, medium that sockets persist because peer idle-close behavior is not established.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: Workshop listing fetches and renders every listing
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `apps/docs/src/app/(home)/workshop/page.tsx` renders `WorkshopRoute`, which renders `WorkshopApp`. `WorkshopApp` calls `useWorkshop`; its initial effect calls `refresh()`, which calls `backend.listAll({ sort: "newest" })`. `WorkshopApp` keeps all returned records in React state and maps all filtered results to cards. The admin route also calls `listAll` and renders every submission.

**Cause and dimensions:** `packages/workshop/src/backend.ts` offers `list()` with a 24-record default page, but `listAll()` calls PocketBase `getFullList(batch: 200)`. Therefore initial listing transfer, client state, sorting, and DOM work grow with the full number of Workshop records: O(N) response/state/rendering and O(N log N) sorting when filters change. The fallback is more expensive: when the listings view returns a compatibility 400/404, `loadListingsFallback()` tries the view and then raw `submissions`; that raw path includes the full `content` field, which `parseListings()` removes only after it was transferred and parsed. No upper bound on total listings or fallback content is enforced in these callers.

**Evidence and dimensions:** The frontend code path and both backend branches were inspected. The normal listing view omits `content`, so the full-content transfer risk is conditional on the compatibility fallback. No live Workshop row count, response byte size, browser heap, render timing, or number of concurrent visitors was measured. The repository baseline has no such measurements. The issue is unbounded by code; severity depends on actual dataset size and whether deployments hit the fallback.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Use the existing paginated backend `list()` for the public listing and load further pages as the user requests them. Keep summary records in the listing response. For the compatibility path, project/select summary fields before fetching if PocketBase supports it, or page the raw collection and avoid downloading `content`. Apply equivalent pagination to the admin view only if moderator datasets warrant it.

**Tradeoffs and measurement plan:** Pagination changes filtering and sort semantics: server-side query options should preserve the current title/description/author search, type, outdated, and sort behavior across all pages. Before selecting page size, capture listing count, compressed and raw response bytes, number of cards rendered, transfer time, and peak browser heap for first page and full traversal. Separately force the compatibility path and measure bytes with small, median, and maximum-length contents. Complexity is O(P) per page with P bounded; loading all pages still costs O(N) cumulatively. Confidence is high in the unbounded code path and medium on material production impact without dataset measurements.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: the global Kapa mascot starts a continuously animated WebGL scene on every page
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `apps/docs/src/app/layout.tsx` uses a default nonempty Kapa website ID and mounts `DocsMascot` under the root provider. `DocsMascot` immediately imports `./scene`, fetches the SVG, and constructs the Three.js renderer in an effect. The launcher is fixed to the viewport, so its intersection observer normally keeps the scene visible. For users without reduced-motion preference, `scene.ts` continues scheduling animation frames while the page is visible; it renders at approximately 30 fps (`now - lastRender >= 32`) even when the user is idle. The scene is dynamically split, but the effect requests its chunk and mascot asset on every page mount.

**Cause and dimensions:** This retains the WebGL renderer, scene geometry/materials, canvas, and associated GPU resources for the lifetime of every page view; it also performs ongoing animation and render work while idle. Page visibility and intersection observers pause work, and cleanup disposes geometry/materials, skeletons, renderer, listeners, and observers. Reduced-motion users get a static initial render. There is no leak indicated by the inspected lifecycle. Transfer bytes for the scene chunk/SVG, retained heap/GPU memory, and idle CPU/GPU time were not measured. The homepage feature is documented as slowly spinning, so reducing idle work changes an intentional behavior.

**Smallest compatible fix:** If measurements show meaningful cost, keep the static logo as the initial state and load/create the 3D scene after explicit pointer or keyboard intent. Preserve the Ask AI launcher, keyboard access, reduced-motion behavior, and the existing dispose path. A less visible alternative is to keep the scene but stop its animation after the greeting and resume on interaction.

**Tradeoffs and measurement plan:** Deferring activation removes the idle animation until interaction and adds scene-load latency on first use. Measure route-level compressed JS/SVG transfer, JS heap and GPU process memory after activation, and a 30-second idle CPU/GPU profile on a representative desktop and mobile device, with normal and reduced-motion settings. Compare current and deferred activation while checking pointer, keyboard, Kapa loading failure, client navigation, hidden-tab pause, and unmount cleanup. The code evidence is high confidence; performance impact is medium confidence because current browser profiles and transfer measurements are absent.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: LDAP authentication failures can retain connected sockets
details:
**Affected files:** `packages/auth/providers/credentials/authorization/ldap-authorization.ts`, `packages/auth/providers/credentials/ldap-client.ts`, and the caller `packages/auth/providers/credentials/credentials-provider.ts`.

**Call path and trigger:** Auth.js invokes `createLdapConfiguration().authorize()` for an LDAP sign-in (`credentials-provider.ts:24-33`), which calls `authorizeWithLdapCredentialsAsync`. That function creates a service-bound LDAP client and may create a second user-bound client (`ldap-authorization.ts:23-31,75-86`). The service client is disconnected only after user and group searches (`:95-109`); the user client is disconnected only after a successful bind (`:76-86`). The provider catches authorization failures and returns `null`, but no `finally` reaches either client's `disconnectAsync` (`credentials-provider.ts:32`). Therefore failed service bind, user search errors, missing/ambiguous user, invalid email, failed user bind, group search errors can bypass one or both cleanup calls.

`LdapClient.disconnectAsync()` delegates to ldapts `Client.unbind()` (`ldap-client.ts:70-75`). The installed ldapts implementation destroys its socket in the `finally` of `unbind()` (`node_modules/ldapts/src/Client.ts:724-737`). Its connection path sets `connected` once a socket is established before bind completion (`:827-875`); the caller's rejected-bind catches do not unbind. This establishes that these exceptional paths skip the operation that destroys the socket. The `Client` constructor does not set an application-specific timeout in `ldap-client.ts:21-24`; the installed default timeout is zero.

**Dimensions and scale:** Each affected failed service bind retained one server socket and one client socket handle after the authorization promise had returned. In isolated baseline workers, 1, 25, and 100 failed attempts retained exactly 1, 25, and 100 sockets/handles. In nine alternating isolated process pairs, the cumulative 1/11/51/151-attempt baseline stages retained exactly 1/11/51/151 sockets/handles in every run; the patched path retained zero at every stage. The synthetic server does not model server idle timeouts, so real deployment retention duration remains unknown. Heap/RSS changes were small and noisy; the measurements do not support a claim of lower total process RAM. Network transfer is the existing bind traffic; cleanup adds a local LDAP unbind request on rejected service binds.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Put each client's complete use in a `try/finally` that always calls `disconnectAsync()`, including bind failure. Keep the current user/service separation, query attributes, LDAP filters, password validation, group synchronization, and provider-level failure-to-null behavior. Avoid sharing clients across credentials or weakening authentication checks.

**Expected tradeoff:** Socket/client retention becomes bounded by the active request and cleanup path. Successful login already performs both disconnects, so its cleanup count should stay unchanged. Failure paths gain cleanup; rejected service-bind latency is measured below, while successful-login and other failure-path latency remain unmeasured. No auth-boundary change is needed.

**Initial worker measurements and limits (before the final lint helper correction):** Harness and raw records are in `audit-evidence/2026-10-11/measurements/ldap-lifecycle.mts` and `ldap-lifecycle-before-lint-fix-results.json`; independent baseline runs for 1, 25, and 100 attempts are in `baseline-{1,25,100}.json`. The paired run used Node v24.18.0, nine alternating baseline/after process pairs, and repeated cumulative stages of 1, 11, 51, and 151 failures. These worker memory numbers include both the authorization client and the synthetic server in the same process; they are fixture totals and cannot be interpreted as production per-client retained bytes or RSS savings. At 151 failures, the median baseline/after fixture values were: RSS 116,711,424/117,174,272 bytes; post-GC heap used 17,755,432/17,133,128 bytes; external 13,119,793/13,224,127 bytes; total stage elapsed 57.77/46.11 ms; per-attempt p50 0.322/0.417 ms and p95 0.567/0.740 ms. RSS and external memory were not lower after the change, and timings were noisy; the deterministic socket/handle result is the strongest evidence. All nine paired runs had 151 retained sockets/handles on baseline and zero after cleanup. High confidence that the enumerated paths previously skipped unbind and that the patch closes the synthetic rejected-bind socket. Remaining gaps are actual directory-server idle behavior, production traffic, post-failure LDAP search-error paths, and successful-login latency. The worker workload completed and wrote the complete raw result JSON; the runner then exited nonzero on a typo in its final status-print variable. That variable is corrected in the harness; the recorded pairs are complete and validated.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding F-1: RSS requests buffer and parse full feeds with 100-way fanout
details:
**Affected files:** `packages/api/src/router/widgets/rssFeed.ts`, `packages/request-handler/src/rss-feeds.ts`, and the installed `node_modules/@extractus/feed-extractor/src/utils/retrieve.js`.

**Call path and trigger:** The public `rssFeed.getFeeds` procedure accepts up to 100 URLs and starts all feed handlers at once with `Promise.allSettled`. Its API schema does not cap `maximumAmountPosts` (the widget editor separately suggests a 1–9,999 range), so direct callers can also request an arbitrarily large returned count. For each URL it calls `rssFeedsRequestHandler`, which calls `extract()` before trimming the result to `maximumAmountPosts`. The installed feed-extractor implementation calls `res.arrayBuffer()`, decodes the complete buffer into a JavaScript string, and parses the complete JSON or XML feed. For XML, parsing materializes an object tree before normalization. Thus the entry-count limit controls the returned entries but does not cap bytes downloaded or work done per feed. The URL array limit bounds one call to 100 feeds, while payload bytes per feed remain unbounded.

The RSS result is cached in a process-local request-handler cache with at most 1,000 entries and the default 10-second TTL. That limits entry count and normal retention time, but each cache entry's size is determined by the requested output count and feed fields. The full input buffer, decoded string, and parse tree are temporary but may overlap across the 100 concurrent fetches; normalized output can then remain in the L1 cache briefly. There is no evidence that the Redis shared cache is used for RSS: this handler is created without a `cacheNamespace`.

**Dimensions and evidence:** During each fetch, response bytes occupy an ArrayBuffer/Buffer allocation and the decoded text occupies V8 heap; parsing creates additional heap objects, and normalized results create another representation. The peak scales with the sum of concurrently processed feed sizes and parser expansion, not only `maximumAmountPosts`. `Promise.allSettled` also retains each settled result until the slowest feed completes. Aggregate feed sizes, peak `heapUsed`, `external`, `arrayBuffers`, RSS, response transfer, and parse CPU were not measured. These memory counters overlap in Node and must be reported separately rather than summed into an independent total. No absolute savings are claimed.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Read feed bodies through a streaming byte limit and cancel the body when the limit is exceeded; limit concurrent feed fetches with a small worker pool while preserving the input/result association and final chronological ordering. Keep the existing post-count and description limits as output controls. A byte cap needs a user-appropriate limit and error behavior because legitimate feeds vary in size; the current code provides no existing cap to reuse.

**Authorization, ordering, freshness, and tradeoffs:** Anonymous and ordinary users have URLs restricted to feeds configured on accessible boards; board creators/modifiers may supply arbitrary URLs. The procedure still accepts up to 100 URLs from the caller. The proposed byte cap would reject unusually large feeds and could reduce available entries for those sources. A worker pool would reduce peak concurrent transfer and parser memory while increasing latency for batches of many feeds. The current response sorts combined entries by publish date and truncates the aggregate, so the fix should retain that output ordering. The short L1 TTL remains useful to avoid repeated fetches but does not constrain a single response's ingestion size.

**Confidence and gaps:** High confidence in the unbounded-per-feed ingestion and concurrent allocation path; the installed dependency source confirms the whole-body buffer and decode. The actual risk depends on feed sizes, URL count, runtime limit, and traffic. No production feed-size distribution or before/after memory, transfer, or latency measurements were available.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding F-2: weekly icon refresh loads every uploaded media blob to compute local icon checksums
details:
**Affected files:** `packages/icons/src/repositories/local.icon-repository.ts`, `packages/icons/src/icons-fetcher.ts`, `packages/cron-jobs/src/jobs/icons-updater.ts`; callers and data shape inspected in `packages/api/src/router/medias/media-router.ts`, `packages/validation/src/media.ts`, and both DB media schemas.

**Call path and trigger:** `@homarr/tasks` initializes the cron group and starts jobs. The `iconsUpdater` job runs on startup and weekly, calls `fetchIconsAsync()`, then keeps all returned repository groups while it loads the existing icon repositories with their icon rows, flattens those rows, computes skipped checksums and pending inserts/deletes, and applies a transaction. The local repository return value contains metadata only, not the source Buffers; the peak full-blob materialization is during `LocalIconRepository.getAllIconsInternalAsync()` before it returns. `fetchIconsAsync()` runs all six repository fetches concurrently, including `LocalIconRepository`. That repository calls `db.query.medias.findMany()` without a column projection, so every row includes its `content` blob. It maps all rows through `mapMediaToIcon`, which hashes the complete content with MD5 but returns only the name, URL, size, and checksum. The media table stores content as a SQLite Buffer blob or PostgreSQL bytea.

The media upload schema allows each file to be up to 32 MiB and does not set a maximum file count. Upload processing already hashes each file through `mapMediaToIcon` and writes the resulting checksum into the icons table when the local icon repository exists; deletion removes the corresponding icon row. The periodic refresh therefore rereads all uploaded bytes for checksum comparison, even though it primarily needs local icon metadata and a checksum already stored for ordinary uploads. If the local icon repository row did not exist at upload time, the updater can also initialize it and backfill icons, so that path must be preserved in a repair.

**Dimensions and evidence:** The local query materializes all media rows and their Buffers together during the repository fetch and MD5 pass, giving a peak raw payload footprint proportional to the sum of all uploaded file sizes. Once `LocalIconRepository.getAllIconsInternalAsync()` returns, its local row array is out of scope and only the small icon metadata objects are returned; raw Buffers are eligible for collection before the updater finishes its later database reconciliation, though actual GC timing is not measured. Those Buffer bytes are external/ArrayBuffer memory; Buffer wrappers, result objects, icon objects, remote repository metadata, database icon rows, and pending insert/checksum arrays also occupy V8 heap. The six repository responses are concurrently processed and their returned groups are retained; remote repositories return indexing metadata, while the local result contains metadata only after hashing. The periodic updater's separate DB icon query loads icon metadata, not media blobs. These dimensions are distinct and were not measured. No live database was queried for media count or total bytes.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Avoid transferring all media contents on every refresh. Preserve the existing upload/delete lifecycle and initial backfill behavior by either (a) persisting a stable local-media checksum at write time and selecting only id/name/size/checksum metadata during refresh, or (b) reading missing legacy media in bounded keyset batches so only a bounded number of content Buffers are resident at once. The first option needs a compatibility plan for existing records and must retain change detection if media content can be updated in place; the current API creates and deletes media but exposes no content-update operation. A one-time reconciliation may be required for legacy records or a missing local icon repository.

**Ordering, freshness, and tradeoffs:** The job synchronizes remote icon repositories and deletes stale local icon rows in the same transaction. The fix must still create the local repository when absent, backfill all existing media icons, and keep checksum comparison/deletion semantics. A persisted checksum uses storage at upload time and makes scheduled refresh cheap; batched reads preserve content-derived checksums but add query/transaction complexity and still hash all bytes over the full job. This weekly job also runs at process startup, so memory cost can recur after deployments or restarts rather than only once a week.

**Confidence and gaps:** High confidence in the full-blob query and repeated checksum work. The process-level peak is expected to scale with total stored media bytes plus metadata, but no row count, total byte count, peak memory, startup duration, or CPU profile was measured. SQLite and PostgreSQL Buffer behavior may differ in transfer and allocator details; the same high-level retained-byte issue applies to both.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: `app.selectable` returns an unused `pingUrl` for every app
details:
**Problem and trigger.** The first time a consumer observes `clientApi.app.selectable`, the server returns the complete selectable-app list. The API projection includes `pingUrl` for each app (`packages/api/src/router/app.ts:118-155`). The UI package's selector directly calls this query (`packages/modals-collection/src/apps/app-select-modal.tsx:27-60`), but neither the selector's cards nor its callbacks read `pingUrl`. Its concrete callers are the board add-app action, whose callback uses only `app.id` (`apps/nextjs/src/app/[locale]/boards/(content)/_edit-actions.tsx:56-72`), and the integration edit selector, whose form's `app` schema contains only `id`, `name`, `iconUrl`, and `href` (`apps/nextjs/src/app/[locale]/manage/integrations/edit/[id]/_integration-edit-form.tsx:47-55, 314-350`).

The same endpoint is shared by app widget selection, bookmarks, the board selection toolbar, new integration selection, and Spotlight's authenticated catalog (`packages/widgets/src/_inputs/widget-app-input.tsx`, `packages/widgets/src/bookmarks/add-button.tsx`, `apps/nextjs/src/components/board/selection/board-selection-toolbar.tsx`, `apps/nextjs/src/app/[locale]/manage/integrations/new/_integration-new-form.tsx`, and `packages/spotlight/src/lib/catalog.ts`). Inspection of these consumers found no `pingUrl` read; they use app identity and display fields such as name, icon, href, and description. Spotlight can keep the query observed during the authenticated session. When an observer goes away, the query cache's default GC window is five minutes (`packages/api/src/query-cache.ts:13`; applied by `apps/nextjs/src/app/[locale]/_client-providers/trpc.tsx:131-135`).

**Cause and dimensions.** The shared selectable endpoint exposes a full app field that its current consumers do not need. Removing it reduces response transfer and the corresponding query-cache/client object footprint in proportion to the number of apps and the serialized ping URL lengths. It does not reduce server query row count or the UI's rendered app-card count. No production app-count, response-byte, or heap measurement was collected, so the absolute savings are unknown.

**Smallest compatible fix.** Remove `pingUrl` from the `selectable` output projection and DB `columns` in `packages/api/src/router/app.ts`; update the OpenAPI description to omit ping URLs. The separate app detail/create/update endpoints retain their ping URL fields. This keeps all inspected selectable consumers' needed fields intact. Tradeoff: any external consumer relying on the documented selectable endpoint's ping URL would need a separate detail lookup; no in-repository consumer does so.

**Complexity, confidence, and gaps.** Low implementation complexity; high confidence that the in-repository UI callers do not use this value. The app result list has no API limit, so the reduction scales with account app count. Validate actual bytes before/after for representative small and large app sets, and inspect the query cache/heap after fetching and after its five-minute inactive GC window if sizing the runtime impact is needed. No runtime measurements were made.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding 1: Board resize writes the viewport cookie every animation frame
details:
**Call path and trigger.** The locale root mounts `ViewportHint` on every page. It writes the `homarr-viewport-width` cookie immediately and debounces subsequent resize writes by 150 ms. On board pages, `BoardProviders` mounts `BoardProvider`; its `useSyncExternalStore` subscription also receives each window resize and batches layout updates to one requestAnimationFrame. That callback writes the same cookie before notifying React. Dragging a browser edge while a board is open therefore performs a synchronous cookie write on every animation frame as well as the existing debounced final write.

**Cause and dimensions.** For a resize lasting `R` rendered frames, this adds `R` synchronous `document.cookie` assignments, instead of the single trailing assignment already supplied by `ViewportHint`. The store subscription still needs per-frame notifications to switch responsive layouts. The extra write has constant space use; its CPU/main-thread cost is not measured here. Both writes persist the same rounded viewport width with the same path and max age.

**Minimal compatible fix and tradeoff.** Remove the cookie assignment from the board subscription and keep `onStoreChange()` in the frame callback. Let `ViewportHint` remain responsible for the initial value and debounced resize persistence. This preserves live layout switching while eliminating duplicate per-frame storage work. The tradeoff is that server-side viewport hints update after the existing 150 ms quiet period, which already defines root-level behavior.

**Evidence and confidence.** Directly confirmed at `packages/boards/src/context.tsx:24-41,103-105,178-180` and `apps/nextjs/src/components/layout/viewport-hint.tsx:8-24`. The duplicate write path and trigger are high-confidence; user-visible impact is likely small and needs a browser trace to quantify. A baseline measurement should count cookie assignments and main-thread time during a fixed 3-second window resize, before and after removing the board write.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding 2: Spotlight filters complete catalogs on every non-empty query
details:
**Call path and trigger.** `LazySpotlight` loads the Spotlight module on first open (or preloads it after one second while idle) and mounts `<Spotlight />` after the open event. `Spotlight` calls `useSpotlightCatalogs()`, which enables the board catalog for resolved sessions and the search-engine catalog for resolved sessions; it enables app and integration catalogs for eligible authenticated users. The app, board, integration, and external-search groups call the same query hooks and run `filterCatalog` as the query changes. For a non-empty query, the helper lowercases searchable fields and creates a scored object for every option, filters matches, sorts all matches, then keeps only the first eight (ten for external engines). This is repeated across each active catalog group on keystrokes.

**Cause and dimensions.** Filtering is O(N) per option scan plus O(M log M) sorting for `M` matching entries, with O(N) temporary score/value allocations; `N` is each full catalog size. The APIs are unbounded in these paths: `board.catalog` passes no limit, `app.selectable` returns every app, `integration.all` returns all accessible configured integrations, and `searchEngine.catalog` returns all available engines. The UI renders only a small prefix. The app-selectable payload also includes `pingUrl` and `description`, which this Spotlight group neither searches nor displays; it uses app id/name/icon/destination. Current compressed transfer size, cache retention, catalog cardinality, and per-keystroke time were not measured.

**Minimal compatible direction and tradeoffs.** For large catalogs, use a bounded server-side search result shape for Spotlight, preserving current scoring/tie order and permission rules, and request results only when the debounced query is non-empty. Keep the existing selectable catalog available to its other consumers. This reduces transfer, retained response data, and client work at the cost of query requests while typing and requiring server-side parity for matching semantics. A smaller isolated change is a bounded top-k selection in `filterCatalog`, which preserves the current catalog cache but reduces sorting allocations/work from O(M log M) to O(N log k); it does not reduce catalog transfer or retained cache data.

**Evidence and confidence.** Query and filter behavior is at `packages/spotlight/src/lib/catalog.ts:17-35,37-68,71-95`; the app consumer is at `packages/spotlight/src/modes/app-integration-board/apps-search-group.tsx:98-109`; Spotlight invokes the catalog hook at `packages/spotlight/src/components/spotlight.tsx:39-45`; lazy mount/preload is at `apps/nextjs/src/components/layout/header/lazy-spotlight.tsx:24-64`. API contracts are in `packages/api/src/router/board.ts`, `packages/api/src/router/app.ts`, `packages/api/src/router/integration/integration-router.ts`, and `packages/api/src/router/search-engine/search-engine-router.ts`. Complexity is directly evident and the API inputs are unbounded. Practical impact is medium confidence because real cardinalities and browser timings are missing. Baseline should record item counts, serialized response bytes, gzip bytes, cache retained size, and per-keystroke CPU for small (10), medium (100), and large (1,000) synthetic catalogs; compare the existing sort with bounded top-k and a server-search prototype while checking result parity.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: bounded JSON response reader duplicates the capped byte payload
details:
The reader first retains each `Uint8Array` chunk in `chunks`, then allocates a contiguous `Uint8Array(byteLength)` and copies all chunk bytes into it. That adds up to one response-cap worth of transient raw-byte allocation during assembly. Decoding then creates a string, and `JSON.parse` creates the object graph. Whether V8 collects the no-longer-used chunk references or contiguous bytes before parsing depends on runtime liveness and GC; peak RSS was not measured.

Concrete path: a request handler or API route fetches untrusted JSON and calls the package helper. The in-scope call sites set caps of 512 KiB for timetable data (`packages/request-handler/src/timetable-url.ts`) and 2 MiB for both custom API responses (`packages/api/src/router/widgets/custom-api-security.ts`) and Traefik responses (`packages/integrations/src/traefik/traefik-bounds.ts`). At the 2 MiB cap, the assembly step can hold the incoming chunk backing stores and a further 2 MiB contiguous buffer. The later decoded string and parsed result add payload-dependent memory. Concurrent requests multiply the transient cost.

- **Trigger and dimensions:** A valid, near-cap response reaching any of those consumers. This is a RAM allocation finding; response transfer is still capped, and CPU remains linear in response bytes. There is no evidence of persistent retention after the function returns.
- **Cause and complexity:** O(M) stream reads and copy work for a response of M bytes; `chunks` plus the contiguous body temporarily account for roughly 2M raw bytes before decoding. Parsing and object overhead are inherent in returning a parsed JSON value.
- **Smallest compatible fix:** Decode chunks incrementally with one `TextDecoder` using `{ stream: true }`, append the final decoder output, and parse the resulting text. This can remove the additional contiguous byte buffer while retaining the byte-count guard. It trades one clear typed-array copy for chunk string pieces and requires careful final decoder flush behavior. A streaming JSON parser would be a larger API/behavior change and is not justified by current evidence.
- **Measurements and confidence:** No runtime allocation, RSS, or concurrency measurements are available, so the user-visible impact is unquantified. The avoidable allocation is directly established by the implementation; impact confidence is low to medium because the strict cap is 2 MiB and traffic/concurrency distributions are unknown.
- **Baseline plan:** Replay representative small, median, and near-cap payloads through the current and proposed readers under the same Node version. Record peak RSS and heap/external memory deltas, allocated bytes, CPU time, and throughput at expected concurrent request counts; verify parsed values and rejection behavior remain identical. Include compressed/streamed transport behavior only if the production fetch path exposes it.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: provider requests retain raw, decoded, and encoded copies while waiting upstream
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `apps/workshop/main.go` registers `registerHomarrProvider`, which binds authenticated `POST /api/ai/v1/chat/completions` to `homarrProvider.chat`. Once admitted, `chat` reads the request body, unmarshals it into `providerRequest`, unmarshals it again into `map[string]any`, validates and sanitizes that map, then marshals it into `upstreamBody`. The same handler synchronously waits for the configured HTTP client, whose timeout is five minutes. The 100-request global in-flight counter is held until the handler returns.

**Cause and dimensions:** The raw byte slice, dynamic decoded object graph, and marshaled upstream byte slice are simultaneously live across quota work and the network wait. `maxChatRequestBytes` permits up to 12,000,000 bytes per request; the map adds per-key, per-value, slice, and interface overhead, while `providerRequest` adds a bounded message/role representation. At the configured concurrency, raw and outgoing byte slices alone have a 2.4 GB theoretical cap; including the decoded map gives a larger heap peak, but its amplification and typical accepted request size are unmeasured. The input text/image checks reduce ordinary payload sizes, but the request-size cap still bounds accepted JSON with structural/numeric data, and the two-per-user cap does not lower the 100-request aggregate. This is Go service RAM; it is separate from PocketBase/SQLite memory, client/browser buffers, network transfer, and upstream response processing.

**Smallest compatible fix:** After producing `upstreamBody`, clear references to the raw body, decoded map, and first-pass `providerRequest` before the potentially long upstream wait. This preserves request validation and provider behavior while allowing those representations to be collected. A follow-up can parse model/stream/message-count from one representation to remove the duplicate initial decode, if implementation complexity is justified by measurements. Do not change request-size, in-flight, or timeout semantics as part of this memory fix.

**Tradeoffs and measurement plan:** Clearing references permits reclamation at the next GC; it does not force an immediate collection, and the outgoing body remains retained for transport. Measure Go `HeapAlloc`, `HeapInuse`, RSS, allocation bytes, GC pause/CPU, request bytes, and time spent waiting at concurrency 1, 10, and 100. Use representative text-only, five-image, structural/numeric-heavy near-cap, and rejected over-cap requests against a delayed local provider. Record container memory limits and distinguish the response-body path (bounded to 8 MiB, streamed or read/aliased) from request retention. Confidence is high in overlapping object lifetimes and concurrency; actual peak amplification is unmeasured.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: listing compatibility fallback downloads full submission content before projecting summaries
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `WorkshopBackend.list()` uses the summary `workshop_listings` view with a page request, and `listAll()` uses that view in batches of 200. On a PocketBase 400/404 compatibility error, both call `loadListingsFallback()`. It first retries `workshop_listings` with `getFullList`; if that also returns 400/404, it calls `submissions.getFullList({ expand: "author" })`. Concrete callers include the docs public Workshop (`useWorkshop.refresh` calls `listAll`), docs moderation (`WorkshopAdmin.load` calls `listAll`), and Homarr management UI (`useWorkshopQuery` uses `list`). The current Workshop migration defines a summary view without `content`, while the raw `submissions` collection permits content up to 1,000,000 characters.

**Cause and dimensions:** When an older/incompatible deployment reaches the raw-collection branch, the entire set of submissions and author expansions is fetched and parsed into client memory, including every full `content` string. `parseListings()` subsequently validates each row as `WorkshopSubmissionSummary`, which drops content only after PocketBase has transferred and JSON-parsed it. For N records with content lengths cᵢ, raw JSON transfer and transient client object memory include O(sum(cᵢ)) bytes in addition to summary fields; a one-page `list()` call still loads all fallback rows before filtering/slicing. This is TypeScript client/browser heap and network transfer, distinct from the Go provider RAM issue. Current view-based operation avoids the content field; the path is conditional on view incompatibility.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Add PocketBase `fields` projections to the raw submissions fallback so it requests only the summary fields plus the author name needed by `enrichAuthor`; PocketBase 0.26.9's installed `ListOptions` supports `fields`. Keep the current fallback, filters, sorting, batch traversal, and page results intact. Validate the exact field/expand syntax against the supported PocketBase server versions before shipping. This removes content transfer and client content retention without silently changing pagination or stale-data semantics; it does not bound the number of summaries loaded.

**Tradeoffs and measurement plan:** A field allowlist must include fields used by `workshopSubmissionSummarySchema` plus author expansion, and must remain compatible with older collection schemas. Capture compatibility behavior on each supported server version. Measure response bytes and browser JS heap for N=1, 100, and 1,000 records with content at small, median, and maximum lengths; compare the raw fallback before/after projection, and separately measure the normal view. Record cold/warm cache, browser, response compression, and transfer timing. Confidence is high that the branch fetches and parses content; frequency and user impact are unknown. The broader intentional `listAll()` scaling/render behavior is also called out in audit 16 and is not duplicated here.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: completed developer-CLI tasks accumulate until the user clears them
details:
**Call path and trigger:** TUI actions in `internal/tui/actions.go` start work through `task.Manager.Start`. Every task is appended to `Manager.tasks` and retained after completion. A task can retain up to 500 output lines plus its progress steps, title, detail, and error. The only normal removal path is the explicit `x` clear action in the task overlay (`internal/tui/keys.go`); task completion does not prune history. This applies to repeated builds, pulls, and container actions during one long-lived TUI session.

**Dimensions and cause:** This is retained Go-process heap, not memory used by Docker itself. The per-task line cap bounds each task but there is no bound on completed task count. It also increases transient allocations: `Manager.Snapshots()` copies the task pointer slice and each task's line and step slices; `Manager.Running()` calls `Snapshots()` just to count running tasks. TUI `applyTasks` refreshes snapshots on task notifications, and `Running()` is used by render/layout paths. The task-state map in `Model` also keeps an entry per ID, including after the manager's explicit prune. No heap or allocation measurements were taken.

**Minimal compatible fix and tradeoff:** Automatically drop the oldest completed tasks above a modest history cap while always preserving running tasks, and remove their IDs from `taskStates`. Have `Running()` count task state under the manager lock without creating snapshots. A cap limits how much old task detail remains available; a direct count changes only allocation behavior.

**Baseline measurement and confidence:** Compare `runtime.MemStats` or heap profiles and `Snapshots`/`Running` allocations after 1, 10, 100, and 1000 completed tasks with representative retained output; record retained heap, bytes allocated per snapshot, and time per call. Confidence is high for unbounded retention and repeated slice-copy mechanism; practical impact depends on session length and build log sizes.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: PR check snapshots are retained for every visited PR
details:
**Call path and trigger:** Selecting the CI sidebar for a PR calls `fetchCIChecks` from `internal/tui/data.go`, then `gh.GetPRChecks`. The TUI stores results in `Model.ciChecks[pr]` (`internal/tui/model.go`), while the package-level `prChecksCache` in `internal/gh/gh.go` also stores each result. The 15-second TTL only controls whether an entry is fresh; it never removes stale entries. The maps are not cleared when selection changes. Repeatedly selecting CI for distinct PR rows/PR-backed containers grows both maps for the TUI process lifetime. On a fresh fetch, both maps reference the same check slice; this is duplicate reachability, not a second copy of the payload.

**Dimensions and cause:** Retained TUI heap scales with the number of distinct PRs inspected and their check count/field lengths. `gh pr checks` output is also captured wholesale by `CombinedOutput` and decoded into a slice during each fetch, so a large check response has a transient output-plus-decoded allocation peak. No check-count distribution, output-size, or heap measurement is available. The `ci` shell command is short-lived and does not itself create long-lived retention.

**Minimal compatible fix and tradeoff:** Keep a bounded recent-entry cache (or only retain the currently selected PR in the model) and evict old entries from both locations; a bounded CLI fetch may additionally reject unusually large output. Eviction can cause a revisited PR to fetch again. Avoid keeping two independent cache policies if one bounded owner can serve both callers.

**Baseline measurement and confidence:** In one long TUI process, inspect CI for increasing counts of distinct PRs and record check response bytes, retained heap, and map entry counts before/after navigation. Confidence is high that entries persist without eviction; impact is medium/uncertain because each PR's check list and normal navigation count are workload-dependent.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: volume-size enrichment captures every Docker volume on the host
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `docker.ListVolumes(ctx, true)` first discovers Homarr volumes, then calls `volumeSizes`. That helper runs `docker system df -v --format '{{json .Volumes}}'`, captures all stdout with `Output`, unmarshals the entire volume array, and retains a map entry for every volume even though the caller only looks up discovered Homarr names. The TUI calls this on initial/full loads, explicit refresh, and after a completed background task (`internal/tui/data.go`); `homarr data` also requests sizes. The three-second lightweight container poll passes `false` and does not run this path.

**Dimensions and cause:** This is transient memory in the Go CLI process: captured output bytes, the decoded rows slice, and the all-volume map coexist during enrichment. The Docker CLI and daemon have their own separate working sets; no claim is made about their memory. Time and memory scale with all volumes on the Docker host, not just Homarr volumes. No host-volume count or byte measurement was available.

**Minimal compatible fix and tradeoff:** Build a set of Homarr volume names from the first query, then decode the JSON array item-by-item and retain sizes only for those names. This reduces output/row/map duplication in the CLI while Docker still has to enumerate its volume inventory; streaming decode adds parsing code and should preserve unknown-size behavior on command/JSON errors.

**Baseline measurement and confidence:** On a host with increasing total Docker volume counts and a fixed small Homarr subset, capture `docker system df` output bytes and Go heap profiles around `ListVolumes(true)`. Compare peak allocated and retained bytes while confirming the same Homarr sizes are returned. Confidence is high in the full-capture/whole-array mechanism and medium in impact because installation size is unknown.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: user maintenance commands materialize unused user columns
details:
**Call path and trigger:** `users list` calls `db.query.users.findMany()` and prints only id, name, and email. `fix-usernames` loads all credentials users and reads only id/name before sequential updates. The SQLite and PostgreSQL user schemas include password hashes, preferences, IDs, and serialized `headerPreferences`; `findMany` without a `columns` projection loads every column for every matching row.

**Dimensions and cause:** Each invocation retains a full result collection in the Node CLI process until the handler completes, even though only a small projection is consumed. Memory scales with user count and the size of per-user strings/serialized preferences. Password values are loaded into process memory but are not printed by these commands. This is command-duration allocation, not a persistent leak. No user-count or heap measurement is available; ordinary installations may have only a few users, so practical impact is likely low.

**Minimal compatible fix and tradeoff:** Use Drizzle `columns` projections (`id`, `name`, `email` for list; `id`, `name` for username repair). This reduces database result construction and retained row width while preserving output and update behavior. Baseline-check query result bytes/heap with representative user counts; confidence is high in the unnecessary projection and low-to-medium in user-visible memory impact.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Findings
details:
No actionable build, startup, production-runtime, deployment, or configuration memory finding was established in this assignment.

The main production image uses a multi-stage build. Compiler tools, Bun, the workspace install, and Turbo/Next build outputs remain in the builder. The runner copies Next's standalone traced output, the bundled CLI, migrations, and the required `better-sqlite3` native binding. BuildKit caches Next compiler and Turbo artifacts; the runtime image does not copy those caches. This supports a smaller deployed filesystem footprint, but this audit did not measure image layers, build peak memory, runtime heap/RSS, startup CPU, bundle transfer, or package tracing completeness.

Startup waits for migrations to finish before launching services. It starts one Next.js process and waits for an exited child before restarting it. On non-root startup, recursive ownership changes are limited to writable app data, the Next cache, and nginx directories; it does not recursively traverse the standalone application tree. `run.sh` sets `--max-semi-space-size=4`, which constrains the V8 young-generation semi-space. This does not establish an overall heap or container-memory ceiling, and no production measurements or deployment limits were available to assess one.

CI uses Node 24.18.0 and Bun 1.4.2. The setup action runs install scripts serially and scopes cached compiler/Turbo state by platform and lockfile. The installed Turbo version is 2.11.7. `turbo.json` declares build dependencies and outputs and excludes `.next/cache` and `.next/dev` from Turbo build artifacts. CI runs an explicit Next build before checking the custom-widget route payload; the checker processes JS chunks one at a time and reports compressed/raw size against a fixed budget. Neither workflow settings nor source inspection provides actual build-peak memory, chunk transfer, browser parse, or deployed RSS data.

The remaining actions and scripts are CI, release, or scheduled maintenance paths. Most either use bounded static inputs (OpenAPI serialization, README table generation, release output capped at 1 MiB) or materialize external contributor/member lists whose practical size was not measured. No production call path or evidence established material retention there. Deployment workflow concurrency/timeouts and independent architecture runners control CI execution, but runner memory data was unavailable.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Direct findings
details:
The strongest bundle finding was the Custom JSX runtime importing the full authoring catalog through `component-registry.ts`. Before the change, the generated JSON contributed 863,195 raw / 89,058 compressed-estimate bytes to deferred client chunk `1no5g3qscy3pr.js` (whole chunk: 871,041 / 92,566). The compatible fix now generates a compact runtime projection from the same canonical catalog and routes runtime registry plus JSX required-prop analysis through it. The projection preserves all 475 descriptors, required props, safety and blocked-prop metadata, binding modes, aliases, and names; the archived parity comparison passed 4,311 binding cases. The full authoring JSON and docs JSON remained byte-identical to baseline.

The after analyzer emits the runtime projection in deferred chunk `04c180k4sfkkp.js` at 234,629 raw / 19,256 compressed-estimate bytes. That is 636,412 raw / 73,310 compressed-estimate bytes less than the old catalog chunk for the renderer path. The full authoring JSON still emits in a separate 866,241 / 90,588 chunk because the board's lazy widget-edit flow reaches the authoring workbench. The async importer chain is `lazy-widget-edit-modal.tsx` → `widget-edit-modal.tsx` → `widget-custom-widget-configuration-input.tsx` → workbench component reference. The production dependency graph confirms there is no static or async path from the full authoring JSON to `custom-jsx-renderer.tsx`; its static path now runs through the compact projection → registry → runtime components → renderer. If a user opens the widget editor, both catalog chunks are reachable: 1,100,870 raw / 109,844 compressed-estimate bytes combined, an increase of 229,829 / 17,278 over the old single catalog chunk. Route reachability does not establish that both chunks are initially requested. Cold-cache request behavior remains unmeasured. Before and after raw analyzer data and selected projections are preserved under `audit-evidence/2026-10-11/production-analyzer-before/`, `production-analyzer-after/`, and `overview_a-after-projection.json`.

The analyzer also measures the deferred runtime namespace chunk `2w_9fr-5dpits.js` at 404,584 raw / 173,103 compressed bytes. It contains 136,747 / 60,460 bytes from `@mantine/core`, 56,638 / 25,633 from `@mantine/charts`, 111,496 / 45,387 from Recharts, 18,776 / 8,822 from `@mantine/dates`, and 28,005 / 9,991 from `@mantine/hooks`. This directly confirms the `* as Core`, `* as Charts`, `* as Dates` namespace imports plus `Reflect.get` path produce a large feature chunk. It does not establish that all of those bytes are avoidable: the generated catalog currently allows 405 Core, 26 Charts, and 32 Dates component names. An explicit generated name-to-component map could make the supported export set statically visible, but may retain most of the same implementation because the allowed surface is broad. Treat it as a follow-up only if comparing the map against actual package exports reveals unsupported modules in this chunk; preserving every currently allowed JSX component is a compatibility constraint.

Weather is deferred at the widget boundary through a literal component loader. Within that boundary, however, `weather/component.tsx` statically imports both `AdvancedWeather` and `CompactWeather`. The analyzer places them together in `3o6sfc2d7bvrd.js` (22,163 raw / 7,279 compressed); `AdvancedWeather` contributes 9,875 / 2,856 of those bytes. The module graph shows AdvancedWeather's CompositeChart dependency in the same async widget load path. A `next/dynamic` split conditioned on `displayMode === "advanced"` would defer at least the AdvancedWeather module bytes from compact weather and would place its chart dependency behind the same condition. The analyzer's current source-to-output mapping does not provide a reliable weather-only transfer total for the shared chart module parts, so the full saving and request delay remain unmeasured. This is a smaller candidate than the catalog split.

The app-level provider graph is intentionally mostly shared. `layout.tsx` composes auth, settings, Jotai, tRPC, Day.js localization, next-intl, Mantine, modal, spotlight, and assistant providers for all locale routes. `trpc.tsx` imports development-tools only under a `NODE_ENV === "development"` conditional and uses `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })`; its implementation imports TanStack Query Devtools. This is a good production boundary. The remaining provider imports are direct runtime requirements of the global layout; no unnecessary provider dependency is proven by source inspection.

Translation loading is locale-scoped at runtime. `translation/src/mapping.ts` constructs a loader map of computed imports for all supported languages, and `request.ts` calls only the selected locale and, when incomplete, the fallback locale. This syntax exposes all files to bundler context discovery but does not establish that all locale JSON is transferred on every route. `NextIntlClientProvider` sits in the global layout, so selected/fallback message data is part of the rendered client boundary. Largest raw locale sources are Greek (464,200 bytes), Russian (439,792), Ukrainian (433,982), and Vietnamese (355,723); these source sizes are not compressed transfer sizes or JS sizes. Keep the locale loader as-is unless the production graph or a Flight capture shows unrelated locale modules or excessive client payload.

`next.config.ts` enables `optimizePackageImports` for Mantine Core, Mantine hooks, and Tabler icons and otherwise does not configure a bundle analyzer or custom client chunk strategy. That configuration is relevant context but is not evidence of a size reduction. `dayjs-loader.tsx` imports the locale hook, which imports `localeConfigurations`; actual localization is loaded through the configuration's locale-specific importer. `mantine.tsx` and `session.tsx` each use Day.js functionality, so Day.js itself is also a shared provider dependency.

title: Finding: every collapsed board card mounts a duplicate form and starts a query
details:
**Reachable path and trigger:** `/manage/boards` renders a `BoardCard` for each board. Each card renders `DuplicateBoardForm` under Mantine `Collapse`, initially with `expanded={false}`. The installed Collapse implementation defaults `keepMounted` to `true` (React 19 Activity hidden mode), so the form mounts while closed. `DuplicateBoardForm` initializes the name to the current board name and calls `useBoardNameStatus`; that hook debounces the name and enables `board.exists` for valid names. This runs even when `board-create` is absent, although the menu action is hidden in that permission state.

**Retained objects and scale:** The form retains its React form state and query observer while the card is mounted. The React Query cache retains a boolean result under the name-specific key after the observer leaves, subject to the provider's five-minute default `gcTime`. For N visible cards, initial page load can create N availability queries; the server endpoint loads/scans board names per query, yielding up to N reads and O(N²) name comparisons. Result payloads are small, so this is a strong unnecessary-work/query-retention candidate, not a large-byte leak. The query count and elapsed cost were not measured here.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Only mount the form after the duplicate panel opens, with the existing `board-create` check. Opening already increments `duplicateFormKey`, indicating the form is intended to reset between openings; conditional mounting also releases its observer when closed. Alternatively, add an `enabled` argument to the name-status hook and gate it on both panel-open and permission state, which preserves a mounted form but keeps its state. Both approaches trade eager first-open validation for a query when duplication is actually requested.
evidence_status: Provisional source observation. final-decisions.md and final raw measurements supersede initial static wording.

title: Finding: notebook retains a serialized copy and rebuilds it on each editor update
details:
**Reachable path and trigger:** The notebook is lazily loaded through the widget registry and `notebook/index.ts` → `component.tsx` → `notebook.tsx`. On every Tiptap `onUpdate`, `editor.getHTML()` serializes the full document and `setContent` stores it in React state. The editor already holds the ProseMirror document. The serialized `content` is then passed back as the `useEditor` content and used for save/rollback state.

**Dimensions and evidence:** For document size N, each update performs O(N) serialization and creates a temporary O(N) HTML string; the latest string remains retained as component state while the editor is mounted, in addition to the editor model. The setter also schedules React work on each update. This is repeated allocation and one duplicate representation, not evidence of monotonic retained growth or a leak. The baseline default content is 4,438 bytes; user content has no bound found in the widget definition. No representative document-size distribution, input-to-paint timing, allocation profile, or heap snapshot was available.

**Smallest compatible fix:** Remove the `onUpdate` state serialization and serialize only at save or read-only task commit. Keep the editor as the editing source of truth and preserve `previousContentRef` rollback/external-option synchronization. This reduces per-transaction CPU and temporary allocation, while retaining one serialization when a save is needed. Validate the save, cancel, failed-save rollback, external update, and read-only checkbox paths before shipping; they were not exercised in this audit.

title: Confirmed narrower prefetch opportunity
details:
`_creator.tsx` groups every `board.items` entry by kind and calls `prefetchForKind` before computing the current viewport layout. `packages/widgets/src/prefetch.ts` handles `app` and `bookmarks` by issuing direct DB reads for their distinct app IDs, then registers `app.byId` or `app.byIds` query entries. Neither helper checks whether the item has a placement in the selected layout or whether a container ancestor is collapsed.

By comparison, `packages/widgets/src/server-prefetch.ts` has `isInitiallyVisible(board, item, layoutId)`, which requires a placement in that layout and walks container ancestors to exclude collapsed content. `prefetchInitialWidgetData` applies this check before starting integration/widget requests. Its initial kind list for resource preload uses the same visibility rule.

The safe candidate is to apply the existing selected-layout/collapsed-ancestor predicate when forming the app/bookmark prefetch groups. Keep all placements and options in `BoardProviders`; only avoid app DB/query prefetches for entries that will not render in the initial layout. The query keys and returned app objects for visible placements stay identical, so auth, API output, query freshness, and client switching behavior remain intact; switching layouts can use the existing client query path. Expected tradeoff: the first switch to a layout whose app data was not prefetched may wait for that lookup. Before implementing, verify the existing visibility helper is reusable across package boundaries or move the predicate to the owning shared board package; do not copy subtly different collapse logic.

This is a proven over-broad prefetch call, but the assigned source does not establish how often its promises resolve before the initial `dehydrate(queryClient)` or how many bytes they add. Measure it with paired boards that have many app/bookmark entries exclusively on a hidden layout and entries inside collapsed containers, comparing query-cache contents and RSC response sizes before/after filtering.
